events.text: A dry summer, and only one spring in the valley still runs clean. This morning the boundary stone between the upper family's field and the lower family's has walked three paces downhill in the night, taking the spring with it, and both families are at the spring with hoes. The headman asked you, as a witness, whether you saw the stone in its old place last evening. You said yes. You did not look. It was a small lie, said because the upper family's youngest is your friend. Now, while everyone shouts, a mist comes off the spring, and out of it walks something like a lion covered in scales, with a curly mane and one horn on its forehead like a white candle. It walks between the two families with its head low. It is walking toward the witnesses.

choices.text: Confess your small lie before it reaches you

effects.log: "I did not look," you say, loudly, to the headman, to the families, to the thing in the mist. "I said I did. I did not." The beast stops in front of you. It lays its ears back flat against its mane and bows its horned head to you, slowly, the way an old scholar bows. Then it walks on, past both families, past the headman, and lowers its horn at the headman's nephew, who has been very quiet all morning and whose own field, you all notice at once, is the one now nearest the spring.

choices.text: Hold to your story

effects.log: You say nothing. The beast comes to the witnesses, looks at each face in turn, and stops at yours. It lowers its head, gently, almost kindly, and the flat of its horn touches your chest, and you go backward into the spring with a splash the whole valley hears. When you come up spluttering, it is already lowering its horn at the headman's nephew, whose field is the one now nearest the water. Nobody helps you out for a while. (-4 health)

choices.text: Speak for the lower family: they have always been honest

ok.log: You step out and speak for the lower family, and you speak well: the old grandmother who never once moved a ridge, the father who returns borrowed sickles sharper than he got them. The beast listens with one ear turned toward you. Then it walks past the lower family and past the upper family both, and lowers its horn at the headman's nephew. Neither family did it. You were right about the lower family, and wrong about the whole matter, and the beast seems to find that perfectly ordinary.

fail.log: You speak for the lower family and your voice cracks halfway, and somebody laughs. The beast does not laugh. It walks past both families, past you, and lowers its horn at the headman's nephew, whose field is now the nearest to the spring. You were defending the wrong question. You go home thinking about that for a long time.

events.text: You were set to mind the family's goats on the hill and you fell asleep under the chestnut tree, and when you woke the little brown kid was gone. Walking home, you have the story ready: the neighbour's yellow dog chased it off, you saw it, you shouted. At the bend of the path, in the evening mist by the spring, something is standing that was not there in the morning: a beast like a lion with scales, a curly mane, and one short white horn. It is looking at you as if it already knows the story, and the ending.

choices.text: Tell it the truth: you fell asleep

effects.log: "I fell asleep," you tell it, and your eyes sting. The beast lays its ears back and dips its head to you, once. Then it turns and walks into the mist toward the chestnut tree, and you follow, and there is the kid goat, caught by its rope in a bramble, bleating. When you look up, the beast is gone and there is only a deep round print by the spring with water seeping into it.

choices.text: Tell it the dog did it

effects.log: "The dog chased it," you say. The beast lowers its head, very gently, until the tip of its horn touches your forehead, cold as well water. Then it walks off down the path, not up the hill, and stops at your own family's pen. The kid goat is inside, among the others, chewing. It must have walked home by itself. You stand there with your face burning and the neighbour's yellow dog wagging at you over the fence. (-2 health)

choices.text: Follow it into the mist

effects.log: It walks and you follow, through the mist, over the stream on the stepping stones, past the chestnut tree. It does not look back, but it waits at each turn. At the old grave mound at the top of the hill it stops, and there is the kid goat asleep in the warm grass. When you look round, the beast is gone. You carry the kid home and say only that you found it, which is true.

events.text: {npc}, an inspector of long service, has taken you on as a junior for one night's work, because the matter needs someone strong and somebody honest and {npc} could not find both in one person. It is the night tea: a dozen inspectors drinking tea in the dark before the gate of an official accused of theft from the relief granary. The white board is ready, the thorn branches cut. Three people could be the thief: the official, who signed every ledger; the official's clerk, who keeps two; and the petitioner who brought the charge, and who, if it is false, will by law suffer the very punishment the petition sought. The brush is in your hand. By the gate, where nothing was at dusk, a beast of grey stone is lying: a lion with scales and one horn. Its eyes are open.

choices.text: Write the official's name

effects.log: You write the official's name in a fair hand. The stone beast stands up, and the inspectors drop their cups. It walks to the gate, and past it, and along the wall to the little side door where a lamp is burning late, and lowers its horn at the clerk who comes out holding two ledgers. You rub the official's name off the board with your sleeve. {npc} watches you do it and says, quietly, "Good. The sleeve is the most important tool we have."

choices.text: Write the clerk's name

ok.log: You write the clerk's name, steadily, and the stone beast rises and walks along the wall to the side door where a lamp burns late, and lowers its horn at the clerk coming out with two ledgers under one arm. The board goes up over the gate with your name signed under the others. {npc} pours you a cup of tea that has gone quite cold, and it is the best tea you have ever drunk.

fail.log: You write the clerk's name, and your hand shakes, and the characters come out crooked as a dog's hind leg. The stone beast rises anyway and lowers its horn at the clerk at the side door. The board goes up. {npc} looks at your crooked writing for a long moment. "Right name," {npc} says. "Wrong hand. Practise."

choices.text: Write the petitioner's name

effects.log: You write the petitioner's name: people who accuse are often the guilty. The stone beast rises and walks, not to the gate, but to the petitioner standing at the edge of the lanterns, and lays its ears back flat and bows to them. Then it walks to the side door and lowers its horn at the clerk. Nobody speaks. You burn the board in the brazier yourself. {npc} says only: "That one would have hung a true witness. Remember the smell of that board burning."

choices.text: Write nothing until the beast moves

effects.log: You hold the brush and wait. The other inspectors mutter. {npc} does not. The night goes on; the tea goes cold. At the hour of the ox the stone beast stands up, all at once, and walks to the side door where the lamp is burning, and lowers its horn at the clerk coming out with two ledgers. You write the clerk's name then, slowly and well. "Patience," {npc} says, "is not in the regulations. It should be."

events.text: A drought year, and the mountain shaped like flame has woken. Fire runs down its southern slopes toward the capital in the night, and you are one of the few strong enough to stand on the ridge in its way. Before the palace gate one of the stone beasts that guard it stands up, shakes the dust of a century off its mane, and walks south over the river to meet the fire. The beast stops in front of you on the burning ridge, a lion of scales with one white horn, its mane singed, and speaks in a voice like water poured slowly into a stone basin. "There is only one water I trust," it says. "A truth you have never told anyone. Pour it on the fire."

choices.text: Tell it the truth you have never told anyone

effects.log: You tell it. It is not a great truth: a small cowardice, years ago, that cost someone a great deal and you nothing, and that you have carried ever since like a stone in your shoe. As you say it, the words go out of your mouth like cold water, and where they fall the burning heather hisses and goes black. The beast listens to the end, lays its ears back, and bows to you. Then it opens its jaws and swallows the fire in front of you whole, and the ridge goes dark and quiet, and you are lighter than you have been for years.

choices.text: Tell it a truth: a beautiful one, that is not quite true

effects.log: You tell it a lovely thing, a truth with one small lie folded into the middle like a stone in a rice cake. The fire hisses where it falls, and then, where the lie is, flares up, and singes your sleeve. The beast does not lower its horn at you. It only looks at you for a long while with its ears up, which is worse. Then it swallows the fire itself, without your help, and walks back down the mountain. You will remember the smell of your sleeve burning for the rest of your life. (-6 health)

choices.text: Refuse: fight the fire with your own art

ok.log: "My truths are mine," you say, and turn your art on the fire: a wall of qi like a dam of air, cold and hard, and the flames break on it and go round. It takes all night. At dawn the ridge is black and smoking and the fire is out, and the beast, which has been beside you the whole time swallowing what came over your wall, looks at you with its ears half back, the way one tired worker looks at another.

fail.log: You turn your art on the fire and it comes through anyway, over your wall and round it, and you are blistered and falling back when the beast steps in front of you and swallows the worst of it. It says nothing about your refusal. It does not need to. (-15 health)

events.text: A drought year, and the mountain shaped like flame has woken. Here above the clouds it is the furnace-peak at the southern edge of heaven, whose sparks fall through the clouds onto the world below. At the gate of heaven's court one of the two great beasts of white stone stands up, and walks south across a bridge of cloud to meet the fire, and you are standing on that bridge. The beast stops in front of you on the burning ridge, a lion of scales with one white horn, its mane singed, and speaks in a voice like water poured slowly into a stone basin. events.text: {npc}, a keeper of heaven's court in robes the grey of wet stone, finds you on a terrace of cloud a few years after the night of the furnace-peak. "The beast you met on the bridge," {npc} says, "lies at the gate of the court and sees everyone who comes in. It has asked whether you would come in once, and sit in the gallery for one hearing, so that somebody in the gallery is a person it has already read."

choices.text: Sit in the gallery for one hearing

effects.log: One hearing: an immortal who sold a river's rain to the highest bidder, and swore before the court that the river had asked to be sold. At the word 'asked', the beast at the gate raises its head, and the whole court turns to look at you, the one human in the gallery, to see what your face does. Your face does exactly what it should. The immortal is sentenced. The beast lays its ears back at you as you leave.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that you would rather be read from a distance

effects.log: {npc} writes that down. "It said you would say that," {npc} admits. "It also said that it is a true answer, and that true answers are allowed to be shy." Far off at the gate of the court, a great stone head turns toward you and then away, politely.

events.text: Since the morning the beast bowed to you at the spring, the valley has decided something about you that you never agreed to: that you are the one to ask. Today it is two neighbours and one hen, which each says laid its eggs in the wrong yard. They have walked up to your gate together and are waiting for you to say.

choices.text: Hear them both out, and say what you saw: nothing

effects.log: "I did not see the hen," you say. "So I cannot say." They stare. Then, slowly, they start laughing, both of them, and settle it between themselves with half the eggs each. Saying you do not know, it turns out, is the thing the valley wanted from you. It is the thing it cannot get from anyone else.

choices.text: Decide, quickly, to be rid of them

effects.log: You give the hen to the one with the louder voice. That night, for no reason you can find, your ears ring like a struck bowl until dawn. You go round in the morning and ask the hen's question properly. The ringing stops.

choices.text: Tell them it was not you who was bowed to, but the truth

effects.log: They do not understand you, but they go away thoughtful, and that is something. The headman, who heard, repeats it at the harvest feast as if it were his own saying, and it becomes one.

events.text: The county magistrate's court, and a case of a sold field and a forged deed. You are called as a witness, a small one, about a single date. The magistrate's clerk takes you aside in the corridor and says, very pleasantly, that it would be a great kindness to everyone if you remembered the date a day later than you do.

choices.text: Remember it exactly as it was

effects.log: You give the date as it was. The clerk's face does nothing at all, which is how you know. The case goes the honest way. On the walk home, at the spring where the beast once bowed to you, you kneel and drink, and the water is so cold and clean it makes your teeth ache.

choices.text: Tell the magistrate what the clerk asked you

ok.log: You say it in open court, plainly. The magistrate goes red and then white, and the clerk is put out of the court by the elbow. It is a small county and a small clerk. It feels enormous.

fail.log: Nobody believes a villager against a clerk. You are sent out with a beating for slander. But your date stands in the record, exactly as you gave it, and the case goes the honest way after all. (-6 health)

choices.text: Give the later date, this once

effects.log: You give the later date. The clerk presses ten taels into your sleeve in the corridor. That autumn the spring you once drank from runs muddy for a month, and you cannot bring yourself to go near it.

events.text: Since the spring, the children of the valley have a name for you: Wet Witness. It has stuck the way names do. Worse, you have noticed something. Every time you tell a lie now, even a small kind one about a neighbour's cooking, your feet go cold, as if you were standing in spring water.

choices.text: Stop lying, even the small kind ones

effects.log: It is harder than you thought. The neighbour's cooking is genuinely bad. But you find ways: "you used a great deal of pepper" is true. In a year your feet are warm all winter and the name Wet Witness is said almost fondly.

choices.text: Lie anyway, and wear thicker socks

effects.log: Thick quilted socks, two pairs. The lies stay small and your feet stay cold. Every winter you are the only person in the valley who does not complain about the cold, because you are used to it.

choices.text: Go back to the spring and apologise to it

effects.log: You kneel at the spring and tell the water about the lie you held to. Nothing answers. But in the mud at the edge, by morning, there is a deep round print, and your feet are warm on the walk home.

events.text: A child of the valley has broken a jar of soy sauce in the headman's storehouse and is standing in front of the headman with a story about a cat. The child's face is exactly the face you had at the spring, years ago. The headman looks at you, the Wet Witness, as if you would know.

choices.text: Tell the child about the spring

effects.log: You tell it all: the lie, the mist, the beast, the splash. The child laughs so hard at the splash that the story about the cat falls out of their mouth entirely, and then the truth follows it. The headman sets the child to scrubbing the storehouse floor and gives you a bowl of rice cakes for your trouble.

choices.text: Say nothing: let the child find out

effects.log: You keep quiet. The headman believes the cat. That evening you see the child walking alone to the spring, slowly, and coming back wet to the knees, and going straight to the headman's door. You were right to say nothing. Some springs a person has to fall into by themselves.

events.text: The lower family from the spring has come to your door. They are in the magistrate's court over a debt they say they paid, and they have no one to speak for them but the person who spoke for them once at the spring. Their receipt was eaten by mice. They are, you are almost sure, telling the truth. Almost.

choices.text: Speak for them again, but ask them the hard questions first

effects.log: You ask them everything the lender's people will ask, in your own yard, until the grandmother is furious with you. Two things in their story move under your questions. The rest stands like a boundary stone. In court you speak only for the part that stands, and it is enough: the debt is cut by half.

choices.text: Speak for them with all your heart

ok.log: You speak with all your heart and the court is moved, and the magistrate rules for them. Walking home, the youngest son admits that one payment, the last one, was never made. You go back alone and pay it yourself, and say nothing to anyone.

fail.log: You speak with all your heart and the lender's clerk picks two holes in their story in front of everyone. The family loses. They do not blame you. You blame yourself, and learn to ask the hard questions first.

choices.text: Tell them you were wrong at the spring, and cannot help

effects.log: They go away disappointed. You lie awake. In the end the magistrate rules for them anyway, on the evidence of the lender's own ledger, which has the payment in it in the lender's own hand.

events.text: Word has gone round three counties that there is a commoner who speaks for people in the magistrates' courts and asks them the hard questions first. A man with a burned hand is at your gate before dawn. He says his neighbour set his barn alight. His eyes slide away when he says it.

choices.text: Ask him the hard questions

effects.log: It takes until noon. In the end he weeps and says the barn caught from his own lamp, and the neighbour was only the nearest person to blame. You help him rebuild instead. It is the best case you never took to court.

choices.text: Turn him away: you are tired of other people's quarrels

effects.log: You turn him away. He finds someone else to speak for him, someone who does not ask questions, and the neighbour is flogged. You hear about it a month later and feel the cold of the spring water in your chest for a week.

events.text: Years after the morning at the spring, you meet the headman's nephew on the hill road at dawn. He has a boundary stone on his back, roped on with straw rope, and is carrying it uphill, sweating. "Not that one," he says when he sees you looking. "Another one. I moved four, in the end, in other villages, before I came home. I am putting them back. It is taking years."

choices.text: Help him carry it

effects.log: It is a long way up and the stone is heavier than any lie. At the top you set it in its old hole together, and he stamps the earth round it, and sits down, and says that since the beast lowered its horn at him he has not been able to sleep a whole night through, and that last night, for the first time, he did.

choices.text: Ask him why the beast picked him out

effects.log: "Because I was the only one there," he says, "who knew. The families were only angry. You were only lying. I knew." He hitches the rope higher on his shoulder. "It does not see what you did. It sees what you know you did."

choices.text: Walk on: it is his stone to carry

effects.log: You walk on. Behind you he goes on up the hill, one step and then another. You hear later that he finished, all four, and then took up the job of keeping the valley's boundary stones straight, and that nobody in his lifetime ever moved one again.

events.text: The village children have heard that you once met a beast with a horn in the mist, and now every lost thing in the village is brought to you: a spinning top, a hairpin, a hen. Today it is a crying girl of six who has lost her mother's good comb and says her brother took it. Her brother says he did not.

choices.text: Take them both to the spring and ask them again there

effects.log: At the spring, by the old round print in the mud, the brother goes pale and the girl goes pink. It was the girl, in the end: she had hidden it to play with and forgotten where. Nobody at the spring could lie, it seems. Or perhaps it is only that nobody wanted to, there.

choices.text: Look for the comb instead of asking who took it

effects.log: You search the yard and find it in the rice-chaff basket, where the hen had been sitting on it. Nobody took it. You are learning that the first question is not always who.

events.text: Grown, you pass north through the high pastures near the frontier where the birch forests start and the springs are so cold they ache, and buy a sheep at a herders' camp to take on with you. In the night it goes missing from the camp pen. The herder on the next pasture, a hard man with a hard dog, says your sheep wandered. You think his dog took it. On the far side of the spring, at dusk, a young beast with a short white horn is drinking, and lifts its dripping face to look at you both.

choices.text: Look in the camp pen first

effects.log: You remember a kid goat and a fence, a long time ago, and you go and look in the camp pen. The sheep is there, behind the hay, where it has been all along. You go back and say so to the neighbour, red in the face. The young beast at the spring lays its ears back, and the neighbour's hard face cracks into a grin, and you are friends for years.

choices.text: Blame the dog, and watch what the beast does

effects.log: "Your dog took it," you say, and watch the young beast. It looks at you, then at the dog, then at the pen. It walks round the spring, quite slowly, and noses open the pen gate, and there is the sheep behind the hay. Then it lowers its little horn and pushes you, not hard, into the cold spring. You come up laughing, which surprises everyone, you most. (-3 health)

choices.text: Ask the beast, out loud, as you did as a child

effects.log: "Where is it?" you ask it, feeling foolish. The young beast turns its head and looks, deliberately, at the pen. You go and look. The sheep is behind the hay. When you come back the beast is gone and the neighbour is staring at the spring with his mouth open.

events.text: {npc}, the inspector of the night tea, sends you a hat. It is a black official's hat of the inspectors' office, and on its front, worked in silk thread, is a small beast with one horn and its ears laid flat. With it comes a note: the office drinks tea every day at the hour of the snake; there is a cup for you if you want one. Nobody in the office, the note adds, may wear the hat on a day they have told a lie.

choices.text: Go to the day tea, wearing the hat

effects.log: The day tea is nothing like the night tea: a dozen tired officials at low tables, reading out complaints, arguing over wording, impeaching a governor between one cup and the next. {npc} points out the empty pegs on the wall where hats hang on the days their owners cannot wear them. There are always two or three. Never the same ones.

choices.text: Go, and leave the hat on its peg

effects.log: You hang the hat on a peg with the others and sit down bareheaded. {npc} looks at the peg and then at you and asks nothing. Later, alone, {npc} says: "The ones who leave it on the peg at the start usually turn out to be the ones who wear it longest."

choices.text: Send the hat back with thanks

effects.log: You send it back. You do not trust yourself with a hat that knows when you have lied. {npc} keeps it on a peg in the office anyway, with your name on a slip of paper tucked into the band, in case.

events.text: {npc} has fallen ill, and from the sickbed asks you to lead a night tea in {npc}'s place: a minister's nephew, accused of taking bribes for posts. The evidence is good but not perfect. The board is in your hands, the thorns cut. And by the minister's gate, where there was nothing at dusk, the stone beast with one horn is lying again, with its eyes closed.

choices.text: Wait for its eyes to open

effects.log: You wait all night. Its eyes never open. At dawn you send the inspectors home with the board blank, and the minister's people laugh at you in the street for a month. In the spring the real bribe-taker is found: the nephew's secretary, who had been using the nephew's seal. The stone beast had nothing to look at, because the guilty one was not at that gate.

choices.text: Hang the board on the evidence

ok.log: You go through the evidence again by lantern light, line by line, and find the one thread that does not hold: the seal on the receipts is the nephew's, but the hand is the secretary's. You hang the board on the secretary's door instead. As you do, the stone beast at the minister's gate opens its eyes, once, and closes them.

fail.log: You hang the board. The thorns go across the minister's nephew's gate. And the stone beast stands up and walks away from the gate without lowering its horn at anyone, and in the spring the real bribe-taker is found, the secretary, and you have to take your own board down in front of the whole street.

choices.text: Go and ask {npc} at the sickbed

effects.log: {npc} hears you out with eyes closed. "When the beast keeps its eyes shut," {npc} says at last, "it means the one you want is not at the gate you are watching. Go and look at the side doors." You do. The secretary is burning paper in a brazier behind the stables.

events.text: {npc} is dying, old, in a small house near the inspectors' office, and has asked for you. On the table beside the bed is a black hat with the one-horned beast on it, the silk worn thin. "I wore it thirty-one years," {npc} says. "I left it on the peg nine days in all. I want you to know which nine. Somebody should."

choices.text: Listen to all nine days

effects.log: Nine small lies, over thirty-one years: a lie to a mother about a fever, a lie to a king about a poem, a lie to a frightened junior that everything would be all right. {npc} tells them all, and you listen, and when it is done {npc} looks lighter, and younger, and says: "Hang it on your peg. Wear it on the days you can."

choices.text: Tell {npc} that nine days in thirty-one years is a clean hat

effects.log: "Clean," {npc} says, and laughs, and coughs. "Nothing is clean. It is only honest about where it is dirty." But {npc} dies smiling, that winter, and leaves you the hat.

events.text: The petitioner of the night tea, whose name you once wrote on the white board and burned, comes to your gate with a cloth bundle: dried persimmons, the good kind, with the white bloom on them. "You wrote my name," the petitioner says. "The beast bowed to me. If it had not, I would have been flogged with the very rods I asked for the clerk. I have thought about you every day since. I cannot decide whether to thank you or hate you."

choices.text: Say you would rather be hated honestly than thanked falsely

effects.log: The petitioner thinks about that for a long time, standing in your gate. Then sets the persimmons down on the step, and bows, and goes. Every winter after, a bundle of persimmons is on your step on the same day. Neither of you ever says which it is, thanks or hate. Perhaps it stopped mattering.

choices.text: Apologise, plainly

effects.log: "I was wrong," you say. "I thought the one who accuses is often the guilty one." "Often," the petitioner agrees. "Not that night." You eat the persimmons together on the step, and it turns into an evening, and then into a friendship.

events.text: You have been asked to judge a dispute between two people close to you, about a missing purse. Everything points at one of them. You remember the night tea, and the board you burned.

choices.text: Wait, and look at the side doors first

effects.log: You wait a week, and watch, and in the end it is neither of them: a hired porter who had been in the house the day the purse went. You have learned the night tea's lesson twice now. The second time it cost no one a flogging.

choices.text: Ask them both to the courtyard and ask them plainly

effects.log: Both deny it. One of them is lying; you cannot tell which. In the end you replace the purse yourself and say the matter is closed. The persimmons that winter come with a note, the first ever: Sometimes not knowing is the honest verdict.

events.text: The clerk with two ledgers, on whose gate the white board once went up, has served his punishment and been sent out of the capital. You pass through a mountain county years later and find him teaching village children their letters in the yard of a poor schoolhouse. On the bench beside him are two old ledgers, tied together with string.

choices.text: Ask him why he keeps the ledgers

effects.log: "To teach sums," he says. "One book is right and one is wrong. The children find the difference. They are very good at it. Better than the magistrate was." He does not seem bitter. He seems, of all things, relieved.

choices.text: Leave him a few taels for paper, without a word (5 taels)

effects.log: You leave the silver under a stone on the bench while he has his back turned. Next year, passing through, you find the schoolhouse has paper in the windows instead of oiled rags, and a small painting on the wall: a lion with scales and one horn, drawn very badly by a child.

choices.text: Walk past: the board was right

effects.log: You walk past. The board was right. But that night you dream of a white board with your own name on it, for nothing in particular, and wake not entirely sure you would have deserved it.

events.text: You climb the mountain shaped like flame again, a year after the fire, and find on the black summit rock a small pool of water that was not there before, clear and very cold, in a hollow just the size of the words you said. Nobody else seems to have found it. When you lean over it, you can hear, very faintly, your own voice saying the truth you told.

choices.text: Drink from it

effects.log: It tastes of nothing at all, like the clearest water, and goes down cold and stays cold, a cool place in the middle of your chest that is there for the rest of your life. On the hottest days of summer, you have only to remember the summit, and it is enough.

choices.text: Leave it as it is

effects.log: You leave it. It is not yours. It is a truth poured out, and it belongs to the mountain now. On your way down you meet a farmer climbing up with an empty jar, and you do not tell him about the pool, and you hope he finds it.

choices.text: Tell the capital about it

effects.log: You tell it in the capital, and the capital comes up the mountain with jars, and the pool, being only as deep as one truth, is gone by the second day. You stand on the dry hollow and feel the shame of it like heat.

events.text: A dry spring, and a northwest wind for a month. The capital's elders are afraid. The beast before the palace gate sends for you, which beasts do not do: a stone runner, a boy of the gate guard, comes white-faced to your hall and says the stone one spoke and said your name, and then said: the truth you told on the mountain. It wants to know if it is still true.

choices.text: Go to the gate and tell it: yes, still

effects.log: You stand before the stone beast at the palace gate and say it again, the same truth, in front of the gate guard and two passing ministers. It costs more the second time. The beast lays its ears back. The wind turns that night to the east, and rain comes in from the sea, and nobody in the capital knows why except you, and the boy of the gate guard.

choices.text: Go, and tell it the truth has changed

ok.log: "It was true," you say. "Now there is more of it." And you tell it what came after: the apology, the years. The beast listens with its head on one side. "Then it is truer," it says, in its slow water voice. That night the wind drops.

fail.log: You try to tell it how the truth has grown and you tangle yourself in it, and the beast's ears do not move at all. In the end you stop and say, "I am sorry. It is still true. I only wanted it to be less." Its ears go back at that. The wind drops toward dawn. (-6 health)

events.text: Since the mountain, there is a small fire that will not go out. It sits in the brazier of whatever room you sleep in like a cat, a single tongue of flame, and eats no charcoal, and does not spread, and does not die. When you are near it you remember, with great precision, the one small lie you folded into your beautiful truth.

choices.text: Tell someone the lie, plainly

effects.log: You tell the one person it was about. It takes a whole evening and it is not beautiful at all. When you get home the brazier is cold, with a little white ash in it in the shape of a horn.

choices.text: Live with it

effects.log: You live with it. It keeps the room warm in winter and too hot in summer. Visitors admire it. You never admire it. In old age you will sit by it for hours, and it will be the only fire in your life you were never able to put out.

choices.text: Try to put it out with your art

ok.log: You smother it with cold qi until the room frosts over. It goes out. In the morning it is back, smaller, and you understand that it was never going to be put out by strength.

fail.log: The little flame jumps at you and burns the same sleeve in the same place. (-8 health)

events.text: Since the night you fought the fire on the mountain, your art has changed. There is an ember in it now. Every cold wall of qi you raise has, at its heart, one red point that was not there before, and that grows when you are angry and shrinks when you are honest.

choices.text: Train with it, until you can read it

effects.log: A year of practice in the snow. You learn its weather: it flares at your own half-truths before you know you have told them. It is a horn of a kind, you realise, in the middle of your palm. The beast gave you a little of its sight, in the only form you would accept.

choices.text: Try to burn it out of your art

effects.log: You force it out over a month of hard training and burning palms. It goes. Your art is cold and clean again. And you find, oddly, that you miss it, the way you miss an honest friend who has moved away. (-5 health)

events.text: A great master of a fire art challenges you before the palace gate, in front of half the capital. The master is famous and cruel and has, you happen to know, lied about how a rival died. Behind you, the stone beast at the gate has opened its eyes.

choices.text: Fight, and let the ember in your palm lead

ok.log: The ember flares every time the master feints, before the feint lands, and you are never where the lie was aimed. At the end the master is on one knee in the dust, and the stone beast behind you lowers its horn, very slightly, and the crowd turns to look at the master, and the master, to everyone's astonishment, begins to talk about the rival.

fail.log: The master's fire is stronger than your ember. You lose. But in the dust at the end, the master's eyes go to the stone beast at the gate, and stay there, and that night the master leaves the capital and does not come back. (-16 health)

choices.text: Refuse the duel: say why, aloud

effects.log: "I do not fight people about lies," you say, loudly enough for the whole crowd. "I let the truth do it." And you turn your back. The master laughs. Then the master sees the beast at the gate, and stops laughing.

events.text: The children of the lane play a game called Haechi. One wears a horn of folded paper tied round the forehead with string, and the others bring quarrels, and the one with the horn walks between them with head low and butts the one in the wrong. Today it is your turn to wear the horn. The quarrel is a real one: a stolen spinning top. And the biggest child in the lane, who everyone knows took it, is looking at you very hard.

choices.text: Butt the big one

effects.log: You walk the length of the lane with your head down and butt the big one square in the stomach, paper horn and all. You get a bloody nose for it after, behind the woodpile. The spinning top is back with its owner by evening. The bloody nose feels, oddly, like a medal. (-3 health)

choices.text: Butt the little one who is crying instead

effects.log: You butt the little one, who cries harder, and the big one grins at you over the little one's head. The game breaks up badly. That night the paper horn, which you left on the windowsill, is found in the morning soaked through and flat, though it did not rain.

choices.text: Take the horn off: this is not a game

effects.log: You untie the paper horn and say this is a real quarrel and should go to the grown-ups. The others are disgusted with you. But the top's owner gets it back that evening from the big one's mother, and next week, when they play again, they let you wear the horn first.

events.text: You are older now, and the children of the lane still play Haechi with a paper horn. Passing by at dusk you see that the game has changed: the child with the horn, before choosing, kneels for a moment and listens with an ear to the ground. When you ask, they tell you it is the rule now. "The real one listens first," a small girl explains, patiently, as if to a fool. "Everybody knows that."

choices.text: Ask who made the rule

effects.log: Nobody knows. It was always the rule, they say. You were there when it was not, and you do not argue. Somewhere, you think, a real one with a real horn walked down a real lane, and the children saw it listen.

choices.text: Kneel and listen with them

effects.log: You kneel in the dust with your ear to the ground beside the child with the horn. You hear nothing but the earth. But you stand up feeling that you have been reminded of something you knew once, and ought to have kept.

events.text: At the year's end a peddler of door pictures comes through the village with a bundle of New Year paintings for luck: a tiger for the gate against bad spirits, a cock for the kitchen, and one you have not seen before, a lion with scales and one horn, glaring sideways out of the paper. "For the kitchen," the peddler says. "It eats fire. Two coppers."

choices.text: Buy it and paste it on the kitchen door

effects.log: You paste it up with rice glue on the last day of the year. It glares at the hearth all winter. The family laughs at you for spending coppers on paper. In the third month a spark jumps from the hearth into the dry kindling basket, and lies there, and goes out, all by itself, with a little hiss.

choices.text: Ask the peddler where the picture comes from

effects.log: "From the capital," the peddler says. "There are two of those in stone before the palace gate, to stare down the fire mountain." A pause. "The capital burns less than it used to. That is what they say." You buy one, in the end, because of the way the peddler said it.

choices.text: Buy the tiger instead: tigers are sensible

effects.log: You buy the tiger. It is a good tiger and keeps off the bad spirits, as far as anyone can tell. The peddler packs the horned picture away. Later you find you remember its sideways glare better than the tiger's whole face.

events.text: The horned door picture has hung on the kitchen door three winters now, faded to the colour of weak tea. Tonight the wind is from the northwest, dry as old paper, and in the neighbour's house a lamp has gone over. The flames are on the neighbour's thatch, and the wind is bringing them your way.

choices.text: Wet the thatch and fight the fire with the neighbours

ok.log: Buckets from the well, wet straw mats on the roof, all night. The neighbour's house is lost; yours is not. In the grey morning you see the door picture has scorched brown along one edge, as if it had leaned toward the fire and stared at it very hard.

fail.log: You fall off the roof with a bucket and burn your hand on a falling coal. But the fire stops at your eaves, as if it had walked up to the kitchen door and looked at what was pasted there and turned round. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tear down the picture and throw it on the fire

effects.log: Something tells you to. The old paper goes into the flames on the neighbour's roof, and the fire bends away from it, as if offended, and the wind drops, and the neighbours put it out with buckets by midnight. Next year you buy two pictures.

events.text: You have fallen in with the village watch for the season: a lantern, a wooden clapper, and a long night walk round the walls. Old Watchman Bae, who has walked it twenty years, swears before the headman that he saw the miller's young helper climb the granary wall last night with a sack. The helper is crying and swears he was home. You walked that wall last night too, at the same hour. You saw nobody. You also, you remember, sat down for a while under the gate.

choices.text: Say plainly what you saw, and that you sat down

effects.log: "I saw nobody," you say. "I also sat down under the gate for a while. So I do not know." Old Bae glares at you. The headman, who is not stupid, puts the matter off for a week. In the week, the sack turns up in Old Bae's own woodshed, with the rice still in it.

choices.text: Back Old Bae: he has twenty years on the wall

effects.log: You back him. The helper is sent out of the village. That night, walking the wall alone, you see at the far end, where the granary is, a great grey shape like a lion lying on the wall-top, its one horn pale in the moon. It turns its head and looks at you. When you lift the lantern there is nothing there.

choices.text: Say nothing, and watch Old Bae

effects.log: You say nothing and watch. Old Bae swears too smoothly, like a man saying a prayer he has said before. A week later you follow him on his round and see him go into his own woodshed with an empty sack and come out with a full one.

events.text: Old Bae has been found out, one way or another, and put off the watch. He comes to see you, old and shrunk, with a jar of makgeolli. "Twenty years," he says. "Twenty years of honest walking, and one bad harvest, and one sack. I swore against the boy because I could not swear against myself."

choices.text: Sit with him, and listen

effects.log: He drinks the jar, you drink tea, and he tells you about the bad harvest, the sick wife, the debt. None of it makes the sack right. All of it makes him a person. He walks home steadier than he came. The next spring he goes, of his own accord, to the miller's helper's new village, to say it to the boy's face.

choices.text: Tell him he should say it to the boy, not you

effects.log: He goes grey. Then he nods, and takes the jar with him, unopened. You hear he walked three days to the boy's new village and knelt in the yard. You hear the boy gave him a bowl of water and did not forgive him, and that both of them were glad he came.

events.text: Years of walking the wall now and then. Tonight, on the far wall above the granary, the great grey shape with the one horn is lying on the wall-top again in the moonlight, as it has been on certain nights ever since the business of the sack. It never moves. You have never seen it do anything at all. But on nights when it is there, nobody climbs the walls.

choices.text: Walk past it, close, and bow

effects.log: You walk the wall right up to it. It does not move. Up close it is warm, like a stone that has been in the sun, and smells of chinaberry leaves. You bow, and it lays its ears back, the merest flick. You walk the rest of your round light as a cat.

choices.text: Sit down under the gate, as you did once

effects.log: You sit under the gate, deliberately, and look at the shape on the wall. It looks back. Then it gets up and walks the round in your place, slowly, all the way, and lies down again. You laugh out loud in the dark, and get up, and walk it yourself.

events.text: Your sect's outer-court elder sends you to the market town with a sealed purse and a whispered errand: buy a packet of haechi horn powder. One pinch in tea, the elder says, and you can see a liar's face change. The elder needs it for the disciples' examinations. {npc}, the seller at the back of a dark apothecary, has a scarred face and very clean hands, and unfolds a tiny paper packet of grey powder. "It is real," the seller says. "That is the problem with it."

choices.text: Buy it, as ordered (15 taels)

effects.log: Fifteen taels, the elder's whole purse. The seller counts it and pushes the packet across with one finger, as if it were hot. "Do not taste it yourself," the seller says. "Everyone does."

choices.text: Ask what the problem is

effects.log: "It shows you lies," the seller says. "All of them. Every little one. A mother's. A friend's. Your own. Nobody can live with that. The ones who take it start seeing enemies at every table." The seller folds the packet up again. "I sell it to elders who want to frighten disciples. I have never once sold it twice to the same buyer."

choices.text: Taste a grain of it, there in the shop

ok.log: One grain on the tongue, bitter as chinaberry. For an hour the shop goes strange: every word the seller says rings true, flat and clear, and then one word, a price, rings like a cracked bowl. You put the packet down. You do not need it. You have heard what a lie sounds like, once, and that is enough to keep.

fail.log: One grain, and for three days every face in the market lies to you, even the ones that are not lying, and you cannot tell which. You come back to the sect without the packet and without sleep. The elder looks at your eyes and does not ask. (-8 health)

events.text: The outer-court elder has used the horn powder at the disciples' examinations. Three disciples were caught in lies and expelled. And then the elder took a pinch, privately, and since then has accused the cook, the gatekeeper and two inner-court elders of plotting against the sect. The sect is in an uproar. The packet, half full, is on the elder's desk.

choices.text: Steal the packet and burn it

ok.log: You take it at night and burn it in the kitchen stove. The smoke is grey and smells bitter, and for a moment, through the stove door, you see a horned shape in the flames shaking its head. The elder never finds out. In a month the accusations stop, and in a year the elder is merely a strict old person again.

fail.log: The elder catches you with it and, seeing a plotter, beats you half senseless. But the packet falls into the brazier in the struggle and burns, and the elder stares at the grey smoke, and slowly sits down, and begins to cry. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell the sect master what the powder is

effects.log: You tell the sect master everything: the seller, the warning, the elder's errand. The master takes the packet and walks with it, alone, to the river, and empties it into the current. The expelled disciples are not recalled. Some lies, the master says, were real ones. But the cook keeps the kitchen.

choices.text: Keep out of it: the elder outranks you

effects.log: You keep out of it. The elder goes on seeing plots until the elder is quietly removed to a hermitage in the hills. You heard what the seller said. You did nothing with it. That sits in you for some years.

events.text: You have a post as a water carrier in the palace, the lowest post there is. Your whole duty is to keep the great bronze jars full, the ones that stand at the corners of every hall. An old servant tells you why on your first morning: "The fire demon is so ugly that if it comes in the night and sees its own face in the water, it runs. So the water must be full and still and clean. If it is low, or muddy, the demon sees nothing and walks in."

choices.text: Keep them full, and clean, every morning

effects.log: You fill them before dawn every day, and skim the leaves off, and wipe the rims. It is dull. It is the most important dull thing you have ever done, the old servant says, and you find you believe it.

choices.text: Ask whether anyone has ever seen the demon look in

effects.log: "Once," the old servant says, "in the dry year. I was here at night. Something red came over the wall, like a man made of coals, and bent over the jar at the throne hall corner, and saw itself, and screamed without a sound, and went back over the wall." The old servant shrugs. "And the stone beasts at the gate were awake all that night. I could hear their bells."

choices.text: Fill them half full: nobody checks

effects.log: Half full saves you half the walking. Nobody checks. Then one night in the dry season there is a smell of smoke at the corner of the eastern hall, and a scorch mark on a pillar in the morning, right above your half-empty jar. You fill them all to the brim that day and every day after.

events.text: A dry spring with a northwest wind, and you are at the throne hall corner after midnight with your bucket, because you could not sleep. In the water of the great jar, very clear, a face is looking up at you that is not yours: red, split like a cracked coal, with eyes like holes in a brazier.

choices.text: Hold still and let it look

ok.log: You hold so still the bucket stops dripping. The face in the jar looks at itself through you, and something behind you on the wall makes a sound like a coal dropped in a pail, and is gone. When you turn there is only a scorch on the tiles of the wall-top, and, far off at the main gate, a bell ringing once.

fail.log: You drop the bucket. The water in the jar trembles and the face breaks into pieces, and you feel heat on your neck as something goes past you toward the hall. Then the stone beasts' bells ring at the main gate, both together, and the heat goes back over the wall. Your neck is blistered for a month. (-8 health)

choices.text: Throw your bucket of water at the wall behind you

effects.log: You do not turn round. You throw the whole bucket backward over your shoulder at the wall, and there is a hiss like a forge, and steam, and silence. In the morning there is a black mark on the wall the shape of a hand, and the old servant looks at it and gives you the good rice from the kitchen for a week.

events.text: You are old now, and the overseer of the palace water carriers. A new carrier, sullen and clever, asks you on the first morning why the jars must be filled to the brim when they are never used for anything.

choices.text: Tell the story of the face in the water

effects.log: You tell it plainly, the red face and the bell. The new carrier does not believe a word, and fills the jars to the brim every morning for years anyway, and tells the story to the next new carrier in exactly your words.

choices.text: Say: so that the water is honest

effects.log: "Honest?" the new carrier says. "Water?" "A full jar shows what is in front of it," you say. "A low one shows the bottom of the jar." The carrier thinks you are mad, and then, years later, quotes you in a petition to the king, and wins.

events.text: The rice merchant at the market has a box measure with a false bottom, a finger's width thick. Everyone suspects; nobody can prove it. This morning, on the merchant's counter, there is a branch of chinaberry leaves that nobody put there, bitter-smelling, and the merchant keeps looking at it and sweating.

choices.text: Ask to measure your rice in your own bowl

effects.log: You ask, loudly. The merchant hesitates, looks at the chinaberry branch, and lets you. Your own bowl, filled from the merchant's box, comes up a finger short. The queue goes very quiet. The merchant breaks the false bottom out of the box with a fist, there in front of everyone, as if relieved.

choices.text: Pick up the chinaberry branch and smell it

effects.log: Bitter, clean, like the smell of a cold spring. When you put it down the merchant is looking at you as if you were a ghost. That afternoon the merchant's measure is honest, and stays honest. Nobody ever finds out who left the branch.

events.text: You keep a stall of your own now. A dry year, rice dear, and the boy who helps you suggests, very sensibly, a box measure with a false bottom, only a finger's width, only until the harvest. In the morning there is a branch of chinaberry leaves on your counter.

choices.text: Laugh, and keep the measure honest

effects.log: You laugh out loud, and put the branch in a jar of water on the counter, and keep the measure honest. The boy thinks you have gone soft. By winter your stall has the longest queue in the market, and the jar of chinaberry is still green.

choices.text: Make the false bottom anyway: it is a dry year

effects.log: Fifteen taels more by harvest. The chinaberry branch is on your counter every morning, fresh, no matter how often you throw it away. By the end of the year you cannot look at it, and you burn the false bottom yourself.

events.text: The king's procession is passing on the great road to the royal tombs, a river of banners and horses and palanquins. By law a commoner with a grievance the courts would not hear may strike a gong at the roadside, and the king must stop. Your family's land was taken by a magistrate's cousin with a forged deed. The magistrate would not hear it; the governor would not; and the gong is in your hands. The guards are already looking at you.

choices.text: Strike the gong

ok.log: You strike it, and strike it, and the procession stops like a river meeting a dam. A secretary comes running, and then another, and your grievance is written down word for word by the roadside while the king's palanquin waits. In the autumn a royal inspector comes to the county in disguise. The magistrate's cousin is the one who leaves the county, with nothing.

fail.log: You strike it and the guards are on you before the third stroke. You are dragged to the ditch and beaten. But a secretary saw, and wrote it down, and in the autumn a royal inspector comes to the county in disguise. (-10 health)

choices.text: Strike it, but tell only what you can prove

effects.log: When the secretary comes running, you tell only what you can prove: the date, the deed, the seal that is the wrong shape. Nothing about the cousin's character, nothing you only suspect. The secretary looks up, surprised. "Most people," the secretary says, "tell me the whole story of their lives." Yours is heard first, that autumn.

choices.text: Lower the gong: the guards look too eager

effects.log: You lower it. The procession passes. That night you dream of a stone beast with one horn lying at the roadside where you knelt, looking at the place where the gong was, with its ears up. You do not know what that means. You suspect it means you will need to strike it next time.

events.text: The royal inspector who came in disguise to your county is leaving, the case closed, the deed burned. At the county border, at dawn, the inspector stops at your gate in a peddler's straw hat and shows you, under the coat, the round bronze horse tablet of a secret royal inspector. Engraved on the back, very small, is a lion with one horn.

choices.text: Ask why a haechi is on a horse tablet

effects.log: "It is not, officially," the inspector says. "The smith who makes the tablets puts it there. He says it helps." A shrug. "I have been lied to by eleven magistrates. The tablet grows cold in my hand every time. I have never told the smith. He would be unbearable."

choices.text: Thank the inspector, and offer rice for the road

effects.log: The inspector takes one ball of rice and refuses the rest. "The gong was the hard part," the inspector says. "I only walked here." And goes, a peddler again, down the road to the next county and the next lie.

events.text: You are lending a hand in a stone carver's yard for the season, and the carver has been given the work of a lifetime: a pair of guardian beasts for the palace gate, lions with scales and curly manes, ears laid flat. The master has left you the forehead of the second one, and an argument. The old pictures all have a horn, there. The palace officials who pay for the stone say a horn is old-fashioned and looks like a wart. And on the second night, in the moonlit stone yard, something with a real horn is standing among the blocks, watching you.

choices.text: Carve the horn

effects.log: You carve it small and clean, a single horn sloping back from the brow like a candle flame bent by the wind. The officials grumble that it looks like a wart. The master looks at it a long time and says nothing, and then at the next feast gives you the best seat at the table. In the stone yard at night, nothing is watching any more. It has seen what it came to see.

choices.text: Leave the brow smooth, as the officials want

effects.log: A smooth brow, a handsome lion, eight taels' bonus from a pleased official. That night, in the moonlit stone yard, the thing with the real horn walks once round your statue, and lies down in front of it, and stays until dawn, looking at the smooth place where its sight should be. You cannot sleep.

choices.text: Carve a horn so faint only the right eye will find it

ok.log: A horn worn down to a swelling on the brow, the kind of thing you only see at a slant in the evening sun. The officials pass it. The master finds it at once, and laughs until he has to sit down on a block. That night the thing in the stone yard lays its ears back at the statue, and goes.

fail.log: Too faint: the officials see a smooth brow, and so does everyone else, and so, in the end, do you. The thing in the stone yard looks at it a long time, and goes away without a sign.

events.text: Years later, at the palace, an old official, very grand, stops in front of the gate pair whose second brow you once carved and says to his secretary, loudly, so you can hear: "Superstition. No document says these things stop fire. They mark where officials dismount, nothing more."

choices.text: Agree with him: it is true, no document says it

effects.log: "It is true, sir," you say. "No document says it." The official, who expected an argument, does not know what to do with agreement. "Then why carve them so carefully?" "Because a document is not the only kind of truth," you say, and he goes away annoyed and thoughtful, which is the best you can do for an official.

choices.text: Say nothing, and walk on

effects.log: You walk on. He walks on too. That winter there is a fire in his own house, small, in the kitchen, which goes out by itself at the kitchen door, where his cook had pasted a cheap New Year picture of a lion with one horn. He does not mention it to anyone. His secretary mentions it to everyone.

events.text: On the pass above the road you know there is a heap of stones under an old chinaberry tree, and travellers going over the pass leave one leaf from the tree on the heap. An old woman who sweeps there says it is where the horned one used to sleep, when it came down from the north, and that a traveller who leaves a leaf and then tells a lie on the far side of the pass will taste bitterness for a day.

choices.text: Leave a leaf, and keep your word over the pass

effects.log: You leave a leaf and go over the pass and, in the market on the far side, you keep every word true all day, which is surprisingly hard in a market. Coming home in the evening, the chinaberry leaves along the path smell sweet for once, and the old woman nods at you as if she had heard.

choices.text: Leave a leaf and lie anyway, to test it

effects.log: One small lie to a salt seller about your age. All the rest of the day everything you eat tastes like chinaberry bark: the rice, the soup, the sweet cake you buy to cheer yourself up. The old woman, when you pass her coming home, laughs until she has to lean on her broom. (-2 health)

events.text: The old woman who swept the shrine on the pass has died, and nobody sweeps it. The heap of stones is drifted over with leaves, and travellers have stopped leaving them, and someone has cut a great limb off the chinaberry tree for firewood.

choices.text: Take her broom and sweep it yourself

effects.log: You sweep it every month for the rest of your life. Travellers start leaving leaves again. Once, at dawn, you find a deep round print in the soft ground by the heap, fresh, and the cut limb of the tree has put out a green shoot overnight.

choices.text: Plant a new chinaberry by the old one

effects.log: A seedling from the valley, watered all summer. It grows bitter and straight. Long after you are gone, they say on the pass that the two trees are the old one and its child, and that the horned one sleeps between them on its way south.

events.text: A sealed order, a bronze horse tablet with three horses on it, and a county to look into: you are a secret royal inspector now, travelling as a salt peddler with a cracked pole and bad shoes. In the county seat the magistrate is hearing cases in the courtyard under a painted wall, an old picture of a judge and a one-horned beast, the paint flaking. And on the stone steps below the porch, where the painted beast would be if it climbed down, a real one is lying: scales, curly mane, one horn, eyes half closed. The magistrate is careful never to look at it.

choices.text: Watch the cases, and watch the beast

effects.log: Seven cases in a morning. Three times, when the magistrate gives a verdict, the beast on the steps opens its eyes and looks at the one who lost, and lays its ears back. The magistrate sweats. You write it all down that night in the inn, by the light of a rush lamp: three cases to reopen, and the beast's ears for evidence, which no court in the land would accept, and which you trust more than anything else you saw.

choices.text: Sell salt in the market and listen to the gossip

effects.log: Salt sells slowly and gossip fast. The magistrate is not the thief, the market says. The magistrate is only afraid. The thief is the chief clerk, who has kept three magistrates in a row and will keep the next. And the beast on the steps? "It came the year the chief clerk's ledgers started," an old woman tells you. "It is waiting for someone to ask it."

choices.text: Go to the beast at night and ask it

ok.log: At midnight in the empty courtyard it is awake. You ask it, aloud, who the thief is. It does not speak; it is not old enough for that. It stands, and walks across the courtyard, and lowers its horn at the door of the chief clerk's office, and lies down again. You go back to the inn and sleep like a child.

fail.log: The courtyard gate is barred and you go over the wall and land badly in a flower bed, and the guard dogs find you, and you spend the night in a ditch. In the morning the beast on the steps looks at your scratched face, and you could swear it is amused. (-6 health)

events.text: The day of the reveal. Your runners are in the crowd. At your signal they will shout the old words that every county officer dreads, the royal inspector is here, and you will walk into the courtyard with the horse tablet held up. The chief clerk is on the porch beside the magistrate. The beast on the steps has opened its eyes.

choices.text: Give the signal, and walk in

effects.log: The shout goes up, and the courtyard goes to pieces: officers diving under the porch, the magistrate on both knees, the chief clerk running for the side gate. The beast does not get up. It only turns its head and watches the chief clerk run, and the clerk, looking back, trips on nothing and falls flat in the gate. You hold the horse tablet up. The painted beast on the wall above looks, for a moment, very freshly painted.

choices.text: First reopen the three cases, then reveal yourself

ok.log: You push to the front as a salt peddler and ask, as a commoner may, for the three cases to be heard again. The magistrate, sweating, agrees. Each time, the beast on the steps lays its ears back at the honest party. Only then do you lift the tablet. The magistrate weeps with relief. The chief clerk is already in the stocks before noon.

fail.log: The officers throw the salt peddler out before you finish. You come back in with the tablet held up and your runners shouting, a little more dishevelled than you meant, and it does the work anyway. (-8 health)

events.text: Years after the county, you pass through it again and stop at the magistrate's courtyard. The painted wall has been repainted, fresh and bright, the judge and the horned beast. The steps below are empty. A clerk tells you the beast left the year after you came, walking north toward the capital, as if it had finished something.

choices.text: Go north and look for it in the capital

effects.log: You find it a year later, lying under the drum tower at the palace gate, bigger now. It knows you. It lifts its head and looks at the horse tablet at your belt and lays its ears back, and you stand there in the crowd of petitioners grinning like a fool.

choices.text: Touch the painted beast on the wall

effects.log: The fresh paint is cold under your fingers, like spring water. In the paint, for a moment, an eye moves. You take your hand away and look at the clerk, who has seen nothing, and you think: every courtyard where it is painted, it can see.

events.text: The inspectors' office has ordered forty new hats, and you have been hired to guard the hat-maker's cart from the workshop to the office: forty black hats, each with a small one-horned beast stitched on the front with its ears laid flat. The hat-maker, an old artisan with thread between the teeth, says the stitching is the important part. "Do it wrong," the artisan says, "and the wearer goes blind in one eye. Not the eye in the face."

choices.text: Ask what the other eye is

effects.log: "The one that knows," the artisan says, and goes on stitching. "Every hat takes a sliver of the beast's sight. A thread's worth. If the beast lets you take it, the wearer sees a little. If you steal it, the wearer sees nothing and thinks they see everything." The artisan bites off the thread. "That is worse."

choices.text: Just guard the cart

effects.log: You guard the cart. Halfway there, in a narrow lane, three men try to take a hat from the back, for reasons nobody ever discovers; perhaps they wanted to wear a face they had not earned. You send them off with bruises. All forty hats arrive.

events.text: At the royal lecture, before the king, a junior inspector has come bareheaded, without the hat with the beast on it. It is an offence: the court is murmuring, and an elder inspector demands he be dismissed. You know this young inspector a little. He is not careless. He stands with his head bowed and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Speak for him: ask him why

ok.log: You ask him, in front of the king, why. And he says it, quietly: that he lied to his mother that week about a debt, and could not wear the beast's face over it. The court is silent. The king laughs, not unkindly, and says an inspector who knows that is worth ten who do not. He is censured, not dismissed. He wears the hat for the next thirty years.

fail.log: You ask, and the elder inspector rounds on you for interrupting, and the young inspector is dismissed. But at the gate afterward he thanks you, and tells you why, and you know you were right to ask even if the court did not want to hear.

choices.text: Say nothing: the rule is the rule

effects.log: He is dismissed. Years later you learn why he came bareheaded: a lie to his mother, that week, about a debt. He could not wear the face over it. You wish you had asked. The beast on the hats, you think, would have asked.

events.text: You stand accused in your own sect's discipline hall: a manual of the inner court has gone missing, and {npc}, a senior of the inner court, swears to have seen you leaving the library at the hour it vanished. You were in the library. You did not take it. The elders are on the dais, the rods are by the wall, and in the open doorway, where nobody saw it come, a beast with scales and one horn is lying across the threshold, chin on its paws.

choices.text: Tell the whole truth, including why you were in the library

effects.log: You were copying a forbidden page of a different book, a small sin. You say so. The elders frown. The beast in the doorway lifts its chin, and looks at you, and lays its ears back. Then it turns its head and looks at {npc} for a long time, ears up, and {npc} begins, very slowly, to go grey.

choices.text: Say only that you did not take it

effects.log: "I did not take it." True, as far as it goes. The beast lifts its head and looks at you with its ears neither back nor up, considering. Then it looks at {npc}, and stands up, and the hall holds its breath.

choices.text: Accuse {npc} in return

ok.log: You turn and say it: {npc} had the key and the hour too. The hall erupts. The beast in the doorway stands, walks the length of the hall between the two of you, and lowers its horn, very gently, at {npc}. You were right. You were also lucky.

fail.log: You accuse {npc} and the elders, angry at the noise, give you ten strokes for disrespect before anything else. Then the beast in the doorway stands, walks the length of the hall, and lowers its horn at {npc}. The ten strokes are not taken back. (-12 health)

events.text: {npc}, who accused you in the discipline hall and was found out by a beast with one horn, has been sent down to the outer court in disgrace and sweeps the training yard. One evening {npc} stops sweeping as you pass and says: "I took it to sell. My family's debts. I would have let them break your legs. I want you to know that I know."

choices.text: Forgive {npc}

effects.log: "I know you know," you say. "That is enough." {npc} stares, and then goes back to sweeping, harder, as if the yard had done something. Years later {npc} is the most scrupulous keeper the sect library has ever had.

choices.text: Help pay the family's debt (20 taels)

effects.log: Twenty taels, quietly, through a third person. {npc} finds out, of course. Nothing is said. But the next spring a bitter chinaberry seedling appears in a pot on your windowsill, and nobody in the sect will admit to putting it there.

choices.text: Walk on without a word

effects.log: You walk on. Some things do not need answering. Behind you the broom stops, and starts again.

events.text: You sit on the dais of a discipline hall yourself now, an elder. A young disciple kneels on the stone floor accused of theft, and a senior swears to it, and the evidence is good. The doorway behind them is empty. No beast. Only you.

choices.text: Ask the accuser the hard questions first

effects.log: You question the accuser, not the accused, for an hour. The other elders are scandalised. At the end of the hour the accuser's story has three holes in it, and the young disciple goes free, and the accuser is sent to sweep the yard. Nobody lay across the threshold. You did it with your own eyes. It turns out you can.

choices.text: Leave the doorway open all night, and wait

effects.log: You postpone the hearing and leave the doors open. Nothing comes. In the morning you hear the case again, slowly, and get it right, and you realise the empty doorway was the point: the beast came once, for you, so that one day you would not need it to.

events.text: A wrong has been done to your family that no court will hear: a cousin hanged for a murder done by a great house's steward, the magistrate bought, the governor indifferent, the inspectors' office too busy. There is one way left. On the gate tower before the palace hangs the petition drum, for the wronged to call the king. The guard at the foot of the tower turns the poor away. You are not poor any more. And under the tower, chin on its paws, lies a beast with one horn, and its eyes are on you.

choices.text: Climb the tower and beat the drum

effects.log: The guard sees what you are and does not try to stop you. You beat the drum with both fists until the whole quarter is in the street. A royal secretary comes, and then a second, and your petition is written down on the tower stair. At the foot of the tower the beast stands up, and lays its ears back toward you, and then turns, very deliberately, and looks south across the city toward the great house of the steward.

choices.text: First ask the beast whether you are sure

ok.log: You kneel before it and say the whole story, slowly, and it listens with its ears up. Halfway through, when you name the steward, its ears go back. You stand up and climb the tower and beat the drum knowing what the horn knows, and nothing has ever felt so much like solid ground.

fail.log: You kneel and tell it, and it only looks at you, ears neither up nor back. It cannot tell you what you want. It can only tell you what is. You climb the tower anyway and beat the drum, and learn later that the steward was guilty and the magistrate bought, and that a horn, unlike a friend, does not comfort.

choices.text: Turn away: a false accuser suffers what they sought

effects.log: By the old law, an accuser proved false takes the punishment the accused would have had. You are almost sure. Almost is not enough to hang for. You walk away, and the beast watches you go with its ears up, and you do not know whether that is reproach or understanding.

events.text: The hearing of your petition. The steward of the great house stands in the court and swears he was at the house's country seat that night, and three servants swear it with him. Your witness, a water seller, is frightened and muddles the hour. The judge's face is closing like a door. And in the courtyard, at the foot of the steps, lies the beast from the drum tower.

choices.text: Ask the judge to let the beast walk the court

ok.log: The judge hesitates, and then, because the court is full and the story is old and everyone knows it, agrees. The beast rises and walks the length of the court, past the water seller, past you, and lowers its horn at the steward. One of the three servants faints. Another begins to talk. Your cousin's name is cleared before sunset.

fail.log: The judge refuses: a court of law does not consult animals. The case goes against you. But as the steward walks out of the courtyard, the beast at the foot of the steps lifts its head and looks at him, only looks, and the steward stumbles on the flat stones, and does not look back.

choices.text: Calm the water seller and take the hour again, slowly

effects.log: You ask for a moment, and walk the frightened water seller through the night step by step: the moon, the bell, the dog that barked. The hour comes out clear. The steward's three servants look at each other. The beast at the foot of the steps lays its ears back at the water seller, and that is the moment the case turns.

choices.text: Withdraw the petition before it is lost

effects.log: You withdraw. It is not lost, so you are not punished. But it is not won. The beast at the foot of the steps watches you walk out, and you cannot tell whether it is disappointed in you or relieved for you.

events.text: Years after the drum. A ragged person you do not know is at your gate: a slave of some great house, who has heard that you once beat the petition drum and won. They want to beat it themselves, over a beating that killed their brother. The guard at the tower turns slaves away. They ask you to walk with them.

choices.text: Walk with them to the tower

effects.log: You walk with them through the city to the tower, and the guard sees your face and steps aside, and the slave climbs and beats the drum with bare hands until they bleed. The beast under the tower stands up. You stay for the hearing. You stay until the end.

choices.text: Write the petition for them, properly

effects.log: You write it in a clean hand with every fact in its place and nothing else, the way the secretaries taught you on the tower stair. The slave takes it to the tower alone, and is heard, because the petition is so plain no one can find a way not to hear it.

choices.text: Tell them the drum is not for slaves

effects.log: They go away. You hear later that they beat it anyway, at night, with bare hands, and that the beast under the tower was the only one awake to hear. You do not sleep well for a month.

events.text: The court has made you a censor for one year, as it sometimes does with a martial lord whose word the king trusts. The hat comes with the post: black, with the one-horned beast stitched on the front. With it comes a custom older than the office: for the year you wear it, you may not tell one lie. Not to the king. Not to your household. Not to the cook about the soup.

choices.text: Accept the custom, every word of it

effects.log: You put the hat on and say aloud, in front of your household, that you will not lie for a year. The cook goes pale. By the end of the first month you have offended three ministers, a cousin and the cook, and the soup has improved.

choices.text: Accept the post and quietly ignore the custom

effects.log: You wear the hat and tell the usual small lies. At the end of the first month you notice the little stitched beast on the front has turned its head on the silk, very slightly, so that it is looking away from you. You do not tell anyone. You cannot think how you would explain it.

events.text: Halfway through your year in the hat. The king asks you, in open court, whether the new canal he is so proud of is a good work. It is not: it was badly surveyed and will silt up in five years, and everyone knows it, and the minister who built it is the king's uncle. The whole court is watching your hat.

choices.text: Tell the king the truth

ok.log: "It will silt up in five years, Majesty." The court stops breathing. The king's uncle goes the colour of ink. The king looks at you for a long time, and then at your hat, and says: "Then dredge it." It is the most useful sentence spoken in that court all year.

fail.log: You tell him. The king is angry, and the uncle angrier, and you are sent home for a month in disgrace. In five years the canal silts up exactly as you said, and the king, an older and wiser man, sends for you.

choices.text: Find a true answer that is not the whole truth

effects.log: "It is a great work, Majesty," you say, which is true of its size, "and it will need great care," which is true of its silting. The king hears what he wants. The uncle hears what you meant. Your hat, that night, sits on its peg facing the wall.

choices.text: Take the hat off before you answer

effects.log: You take the hat off, set it on the floor beside you, and say the canal is magnificent. Every censor in the court looks at the hat on the floor. It is the loudest thing anyone says that year.

events.text: The year is over. You take the hat off for the last time and hold it in your hands. The little beast stitched on the front looks back at you. Your household is waiting to see what you will do with it, and so, you suspect, is something lying before the palace gate.

choices.text: Give it back to the office

effects.log: You give it back. The office hangs it on a peg. A year without a lie leaves you with a strange habit: you pause before you speak, a breath's length. Nobody else notices. You notice it every time, all your life.
