choices.text: Keep wearing it, without the post

effects.log: You keep it, and wear it at home, and keep the custom. People begin to come to you for answers they could get nowhere else. It is lonelier than you expected, and better.

choices.text: Say one small lie at once, to be free

effects.log: "I did not miss lying at all," you tell the cook. The cook laughs out loud. So do you. The hat goes on the shelf, and you are glad you wore it, and glad it is off.

events.text: {npc}, who leads the stronger of the two factions at court, has asked you to supper and come to the point over the second cup. "The beast before the gate," {npc} says. "It lowers its horn at liars. Our enemies are liars. A person strong enough to lead it into the right hall at the right hour, on a silver chain, would be very well rewarded." A chain of heavy silver lies coiled on the table between the dishes.

choices.text: Refuse, and say why

effects.log: "If it points where you lead it," you say, "it is not pointing." {npc} smiles politely and does not argue. That night, walking home past the palace gate, you see the stone beasts there in the moonlight, and one of them, you would swear, has its ears laid back toward you.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether the faction has any liars of its own

effects.log: {npc} laughs, really laughs, for the first time all evening. "Of course," {npc} says. "That is why it must be on a chain." The silver chain goes back into its box. You leave with the strong feeling that you have been more honest than {npc} has heard in years, and that {npc} enjoyed it.

choices.text: Take the chain, and the reward (60 taels)

effects.log: Sixty taels in advance and the chain in a lacquer box. You lie awake with the box at the foot of your bed. It is very heavy. You find you cannot imagine, however hard you try, the moment of putting it round that neck.

events.text: The night {npc} chose. You stand before the palace gate at the hour of the rat with the silver chain in your hands. The beast lies there, enormous, grey-white, its one horn pale under the moon. It opens its eyes. It does not get up. It simply looks at the chain, and then at you.

choices.text: Put the chain round its neck

ok.log: You get the chain round its neck. It lets you. Then it stands, and the silver chain falls off it in pieces like a broken string of coins, every link snapped, and it lies down again. You go back to {npc} with the pieces. {npc} looks at them a long time, and pays you the rest, and never speaks to you again. (-15 health)

fail.deathCause: a silver chain at the palace gate
fail.log: It stands. That is all it does. You are under it when it stands.

choices.text: Drop the chain at its feet and walk away

effects.log: You drop it at its feet and walk away without looking back. In the morning the gate guards find a silver chain on the flagstones, melted into a single lump as if it had been held in a fire. You send {npc} the sixty taels back. Nothing is ever said about it.

choices.text: Tell it who sent you

effects.log: You tell it everything: {npc}, the supper, the sixty taels. It listens with its ears up. When you finish, it stands, and walks, slowly, past you, into the city, and the next morning there is a deep round print in the dust before {npc}'s gate and nothing else. {npc} leaves the capital within the month.

events.text: {npc}, a broker of rare things who never gives a client's name, has an offer for a person of your strength: the horn of the beast before the palace gate. A sect wants it for a powder. The price is enough to found a house. "It does not fight," {npc} says. "It only sees. That is why nobody has managed it. You cannot sneak up on something that sees."

choices.text: Take the job

effects.log: You take the advance and the saw, a thin blade of black iron fine enough to cut a hair. That night you sit in the inn and look at it and feel exactly as you felt as a child the night before you stole from the kitchen. You tell yourself this is different. It is not.

choices.text: Refuse, and ask {npc} which sect

ok.log: {npc} does not give names. But {npc} likes you, it turns out, and says only: "A sect whose elders cannot sleep." You know which one. Every great martial house has heard of the elders on that mountain who see enemies in their own tea.

fail.log: {npc} smiles and does not answer, and the next week someone else takes the job. You hear later that they never reached the gate.

choices.text: Refuse, and walk to the gate to warn it

effects.log: You go to the gate at midnight to warn it. It is awake. It looks at you, and you have the very clear impression that it knew before you did. Still: it lays its ears back. A warning given to someone who already knows is still a kindness.

events.text: The night of the theft. You are across the flagstones before the palace gate in the dark, silent as a falling leaf, the black iron saw in your hand. The beast lies with its eyes open. It has watched you come the whole way, from the far end of the avenue. It has not moved.

choices.text: Cut

ok.log: You lay the blade on the horn and draw it once. It goes in a hair's breadth. The beast does not move. And you see, as clearly as you have ever seen anything, every lie you have ever told, one after another, in order, all of them, from the kitchen when you were a child onward, and you drop the saw and run, and are sick in the gutter at the end of the avenue. (-18 health)

fail.deathCause: the beast before the palace gate
fail.log: It raises its head. Only that. The flagstones open under you like water.

choices.text: Put the saw down on the flagstones and sit

effects.log: You put the saw down and sit on the cold stones in front of it, cross-legged, like a disciple, until dawn. It looks at you all night with its ears neither back nor up. When the sun rises it lays them back, once, and closes its eyes. You walk to {npc} and give back the advance.

choices.text: Ask it to let you take only a sliver

effects.log: You ask it, aloud, absurdly, for a sliver. It looks at you for a long time. Then it lowers its head until the horn is a hand's breadth from your face, and you see that the tip is already chipped, worn, used, and you understand that every sliver it has ever given was given, never taken. You go home with nothing.

events.text: Years after the night at the gate, a sect on a far mountain sends you an invitation to a banquet: the elders who cannot sleep. On the high table, in a silver box, they show you their great treasure, a pinch of grey powder. "Haechi horn," the eldest says. "Real. Bought dear." The elder's eyes are red-rimmed and do not stop moving.

choices.text: Tell them it will never let them sleep

effects.log: "It shows you every lie," you say. "All of them. Nobody can live in that." The eldest stares at you, then at the box, and then, very slowly, closes it, and asks you, as one old person to another, how a person learns to sleep again. You stay a month and teach them to sit still.

choices.text: Look closely at the powder

ok.log: You look closely and see it: ground ram's horn and chalk. It was never real. The elders have been driving themselves mad on a story. You tell them, and the eldest weeps with relief, and sleeps that night for the first time in years.

fail.log: You cannot tell. You leave without touching it, and the elders watch you go with red eyes, certain that you are plotting.

events.text: You have been made deputy to the Inspector-General, and the embroiderer has come to fit the chest badge of your office: a square of dark silk with a one-horned beast stitched on it in white and gold, ears flat. The embroiderer, an old woman with very clear eyes, holds the needle over the last stitch, the eye. "Shall I put the eye in?" she asks. "Some prefer it closed. It is easier to wear."

choices.text: Tell her to put the eye in

effects.log: She stitches the eye in, one bright knot of white thread. When you put the badge on, the room goes very slightly clearer, as if a window had been washed. You wear it for years. On days when you lie, the badge itches. On days when someone lies to you, it goes cold.

choices.text: Ask her why anyone would want it closed

effects.log: "Because then it cannot see what you do," she says, "either." She waits. You tell her to put the eye in. She smiles as if she had won a small bet.

choices.text: Have it stitched closed

effects.log: She stitches the eye closed, a neat curved line. The badge is handsome. It is easy to wear. For years you wear it and never once feel anything from it, and in your old age you find yourself wishing it had looked.

events.text: Fire in the capital on a night of northwest wind: a servant's lamp in a lane of thatched houses, and the wind has taken it, and now three lanes are burning toward the market. The ward watch's buckets are, someone screams, full of sand. You are on a roof with your art raised, holding a wall of cold air against the flames, and at the far end of the lane, in the smoke, a great grey-white beast with a bronze bell at its throat walks into the fire with its jaws open.

choices.text: Hold your end and let it hold the other

ok.log: You hold your end of the lane all night. At the other end the beast swallows fire, mouthful after mouthful, and the bell at its throat rings each time a roof falls, so that the people in the next lane run before it reaches them. At dawn the fire is out at the market wall. The beast walks past you through the smoke, blackened to the shoulders, and lays its ears back as it goes.

fail.log: Your wall breaks and a burning beam takes you across the back. You fall into the lane. Something huge stands over you, and the heat goes away, and when you can see again the beast is swallowing the fire that was falling on you, and its bell is ringing and ringing. (-18 health)

choices.text: Go down and get the people out

effects.log: You leave the fire to the beast and go through the burning lanes door by door, carrying out the old and the small. At each door you open, the bell at the beast's throat rings once, as if it were counting. By dawn it has rung forty-one times. Forty-one people are sitting on the market steps wrapped in blankets.

choices.text: Find out who filled the buckets with sand

effects.log: While the others fight the fire, you go to the watch-house and look in the store. Sand in every bucket, and fresh. The captain of the ward watch arrives at a run, sees you, and stops. You do not need a horn to see it. In the morning, the beast walks past the watch-house on its way back to the gate, and lowers its horn at the door as it passes, and the captain is gone by noon.

events.text: After the great fire, the court founds an office for fire: buckets in every ward, ladders, hooks, men who sleep in their clothes. They ask you, who fought in the lanes beside the beast, to be its first captain.

choices.text: Take the post, and check every bucket yourself

effects.log: You check every bucket in the capital in the first month, personally, with your own hand in the water. The men laugh at you behind their hands. Then there is a fire in the dry season, and every bucket is full of water, and the fire is out by the second bell. Nobody laughs after that.

choices.text: Say the post should go to someone who cannot be bought

effects.log: "Who?" the minister asks. "Somebody who has nothing anyone wants," you say. They choose an old water carrier from the palace who has kept the bronze jars full for forty years. It is the best appointment the court makes that decade.

events.text: Years as captain of the fire office. In a dry spring the bell at the throat of the beast before the gate begins to hum, very low, a sound you feel in your teeth more than hear. The old firemen say it hums when the city's hidden guilt is piled too high, like dry wood under the roofs.

choices.text: Wet the roofs of the whole capital

effects.log: You send every man in the office over every roof in the city with buckets for a week. It is mad, and expensive, and the ministers complain. The humming does not stop. But there is no fire that spring, and you think perhaps that is all the wet roofs could do: not cure it, only hold it.

choices.text: Ask the beast what is piled under the roofs

effects.log: You stand before it at the gate and ask. It cannot answer in words. But it turns its head and looks, one after another, at five great houses in the city, and you go to each of them and ask questions, and two of them have things to hide, and when those come out, the humming stops.

events.text: A stranger with very clear eyes is waiting in your garden at night, in plain grey clothes, and you know before the stranger speaks that this is no stranger: the eyes do not blink, and there is a faint smell of chinaberry. "You were in the palace the night the scholars were arrested," the stranger says, in a voice like water poured slowly. "You know the list was written before the plot was discovered. Tomorrow the court will hear the case. I cannot testify. I am not a person. You are."

choices.text: Agree to testify against your own king

effects.log: The stranger lays both ears back, which on a human face looks like nothing at all, a slight flattening of the hair at the temples, and is gone. You do not sleep. In the morning you dress in your best robes as if for your own funeral.

choices.text: Ask what will happen to you

effects.log: "I do not know," the stranger says. "I see what is, not what will be. What is: there are four scholars in the cells, three of them honest, and you are the only one who saw the list's date." It waits. You find, to your own surprise, that you are nodding.

choices.text: Refuse: a subject does not accuse a king

effects.log: The stranger does not argue. It only looks at you for a long time with those unblinking eyes, ears neither up nor back, and then walks out of your garden through the wall as if the wall were mist. Three of the four scholars are executed in the spring.

events.text: The hearing of the four scholars, the king on the dais, the ministers in rows. You rise to speak, and the whole hall knows what you are about to do. Outside the hall, at the gate, the bell at the throat of the stone beast has begun, very softly, to ring.

choices.text: Say the date of the list, and nothing else

ok.log: One date, plainly. The ministers who wrote the list go white. The king looks at you for a long, long time, and then, to the astonishment of everyone, asks for the list itself, and reads the date with his own eyes, and orders three of the scholars released before the bell at the gate has stopped ringing.

fail.log: You say the date. The king does not want to hear it. You are stripped of rank in the hall and sent to a far province. But the date is in the record, and three years later a new king reads it, and the three scholars, those still living, come home. (-15 health)

choices.text: Say everything you saw that night

effects.log: You say all of it: the date, the room, who held the brush. It is too much for the hall to swallow at once, and the king adjourns, furious. But that night the stone beast's bell rings and rings, and the next morning two ministers have fled the capital, and the scholars are quietly let out by a back gate.

events.text: Years after the hearing, a scholar you do not recognise, grey and thin, comes to your gate. It is one of the three. "I have been trying for ten years to decide what to give you," the scholar says. "In the end I wrote down everything that happened in those cells, exactly, with nothing added. It is the only thing I own that is entirely true."

choices.text: Take it, and read it

effects.log: It is a hard book. It is not beautiful. Every word in it is so plain it might have been written with a horn instead of a brush. You keep it beside your bed, and you read a page of it whenever you are tempted to make anything sound better than it was.

choices.text: Ask the scholar to give it to the court archive instead

effects.log: The scholar thinks, and agrees. It goes into the archive with the court records. A hundred years later it is the only account of that reign that every historian trusts.

events.text: Heaven is angry with the capital: a king who lied to heaven at the great rite about a famine he had caused. Fire falls out of a red sky in long streaks, onto the roofs, the markets, the palace. You are one of the few people under heaven strong enough to stand in it. Before the palace gate the great beast with the bell is standing, not swallowing, looking up at the sky with its ears flat back. It looks at you. It cannot hold this alone.

choices.text: Stand beside it and hold the sky with your art

ok.log: You raise your art against heaven's fire, and for a night you hold a roof of cold over the whole palace quarter, and the beast beside you swallows what comes through. At dawn the sky clears. The capital is scorched at its edges and whole at its heart. The beast's bell has cracked, a hairline, from ringing.

fail.log: You hold it as long as you can, and then a streak of heaven's fire comes through your art like a spear through paper, and the beast steps over you and takes it on its own back. You wake in the morning under its chin. Half the capital is ash. The other half stands. (-25 health)

choices.text: Go to the king and make him confess the lie

ok.log: You walk into the burning palace and find the king under a table, and drag him out to the open court, and make him say it to the red sky: the famine, the granaries, the lie at the rite. As the last word leaves his mouth, the fire stops falling. The beast at the gate lays its ears back. You realise it was waiting for that.

fail.log: The king will not confess. You are thrown out of the palace by his guards with your hair on fire. But the fire stops at dawn anyway, and the next month the king abdicates, and nobody but you and the beast at the gate knows why. (-15 health)

choices.text: Save who you can and leave the palace to heaven

effects.log: You leave the palace to heaven and the beast, and carry people out of the burning market until you cannot lift your arms. The palace burns. The market, mostly, does not. You are not sure, afterward, whether you chose right. The beast, passing you the next morning, black to the horn, does not tell you.

events.text: The bell at the throat of the beast before the gate has a crack in it since the night heaven burned the capital. It rings flat now, a dull sound. The bell-founders of the capital have been asked to recast it, and none of them will touch it. They ask you, who stood beside it, what to do.

choices.text: Leave it cracked: let it ring flat

effects.log: "Leave it," you say. "It cracked holding the sky. Let it ring like something that did." The founders are relieved. The bell rings flat for a hundred years, and the capital learns to hear the flatness as a kind of honesty, the sound of a thing that has been tested.

choices.text: Ask the beast itself

effects.log: You stand before it and ask. It lowers its head and rubs the cracked bell, once, against your shoulder. It rings, flat. Then it lays its ears back. You tell the founders it is content. You are fairly sure that is the truth.

events.text: A voice like water poured slowly into a stone basin comes to you on your mountain, though no one is there. It is the beast from before the palace gate, older now than any beast you know of. "I am going up," it says. "Heaven's court has a seat at the judge's feet that has been empty since the first judge. I am asked to take it. Someone below should see me go, who can say afterward exactly what they saw."

choices.text: Go to the palace gate and watch it climb

effects.log: At dawn, before the gate, the great grey-white beast stands, shakes itself, and walks up into the air on a stair of cloud that was not there a moment before. It climbs slowly. At the top, very small, it lies down at the foot of something too bright to look at. The stone it lay on for three hundred years is cold under your hand.

choices.text: Watch from your own mountain, alone

effects.log: From your mountain the stair of cloud is a thread of white over the far capital, and the beast a grain of rice climbing it. You watch until it reaches the top. Then you write down, exactly, what you saw: no more, no less. It is the shortest thing you ever write.

events.text: The court of the capital has heard that you saw the beast before the gate go up to heaven, and wants your account for the histories. A minister has drafted it for you. It is very fine: thunder, a host of immortals, the king's virtue mentioned four times. It only needs your seal.

choices.text: Refuse the draft and give them your own

effects.log: You give them yours: a beast stood up and climbed and lay down at the top. The minister is appalled at how little there is in it. The histories print the minister's. But your plain account survives in a temple library, and it is the one people still copy.

choices.text: Seal it: let the court have its story

effects.log: You seal it. That night you dream of a beast on a stair of cloud stopping, halfway up, to turn its head and look at you, ears up. You wake knowing you will never again be the one who saw it go. You are the one who signed the thunder.

events.text: A creature has walked into the capital eating iron: hinges, nails, ploughshares, the spearheads of the guard. Arrows bounce off it. Blades go into its mouth. An old sage at court has said there is only one thing that can kill it, and that is fire. The court has turned, all at once, to the beast before the gate that has held fire back from the capital for three hundred years, and asked it to let the fire out. And they have asked you, who can stand in fire, to carry the beast's answer.

choices.text: Carry the answer it gives: no

effects.log: The beast looks at you a long time, then shakes its head once, slowly, and its bell rings. You carry that to the court. "Fire does not choose," you tell the ministers. "It would kill the iron-eater and the market and the children in the market." You go out yourself that night and lead the creature out of the city with a cart of scrap iron, step by step, all the way to the hills.

choices.text: Argue with the beast: this once, let it out

ok.log: You argue all night. At dawn the beast stands and walks out of the city to the hill where the iron-eater sleeps, and opens its jaws, and breathes out one ember, only one, that it has held for three hundred years. The iron-eater burns red and goes still. The beast comes back and lies down, and does not look at you for a year.

fail.log: It will not. You argue until you shout, and it lowers its horn, gently, at you, and you understand that you were asking it to lie: to pretend fire can be aimed. You lead the iron-eater out of the city yourself with a cart of scrap. It bites you twice on the way. (-10 health)

events.text: In the Upper Realm there is a road of courtyards, one after another, each the courtyard of some court of heaven: rain, harvests, the dead, rivers, debts. On every wall of every courtyard is painted a beast with one horn, and as you walk through, every painted eye follows you. {npc}, an immortal clerk with ink on both sleeves, falls into step beside you. "Do not worry," {npc} says. "They watch everyone. It is only that, here, they can see."

choices.text: Walk on, and let them look

effects.log: You walk the whole road of courtyards with every painted eye on you. It is like walking bareheaded through a hall of elders, at first. By the fortieth courtyard it is like walking through rain: you get used to it, and then you find it clean. At the end {npc} bows and says you are one of very few who did not hurry.

choices.text: Stop before one painting and look back at it

ok.log: You stop and meet its painted gaze. After a long while the paint lays its ears back. {npc} drops a brush. "They do that," {npc} says, "perhaps once in a hundred years. For people who looked back."

fail.log: You stare at it and it stares at you, and you blink first, and you are oddly ashamed. {npc} says kindly that everyone blinks first. Almost everyone.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the paintings see

effects.log: "Whether you mean what you say," {npc} says. "Nothing else. Not whether you are good. Not whether you are right. Only whether your mouth and your heart are the same shape." {npc} considers. "Most immortals find that the hardest question there is."

events.text: {npc}, the clerk of the painted courtyards, asks a favour. A painting in the courtyard of debts has gone wrong: its eyes have closed, and nobody in heaven can open them, and the court of debts has been making mistakes ever since. "It needs someone to say something true to it," {npc} says. "Something nobody in that court has said for a very long time."

choices.text: Tell it what you owe, and to whom

effects.log: You stand before the painting and list your debts aloud: not silver, the other kind. A teacher never thanked. A friend let down. A promise kept late. When you finish, the painted eyes are open. The clerks of the court of debts come out of their offices and stand in the courtyard in silence, and then, one by one, begin to list their own.

choices.text: Tell it the court of debts is cheating

ok.log: You say it loudly, in front of the court of debts: three of its clerks have been writing the poor's debts heavy and the rich's light. The painted eyes snap open. The three clerks are gone by evening. {npc} says it is the first time a visitor has opened a painting by accusing the court that owns it.

fail.log: You say it, and the court of debts throws you out of the courtyard for slander. But the painting's eyes open a crack as you go, and {npc} says that is enough to start with. (-10 health)

events.text: Far below, in the world you came from, a magistrate's courtyard has a painted wall: a judge and a horned beast, faded nearly to nothing. From the road of courtyards in heaven, if you look down through a gap in the clouds, you can see it, and you realise it is the same painting as all the others, the same beast, looking up.

choices.text: Send a little of your qi down to freshen the paint

effects.log: A thread of qi, down through the clouds. The paint on the far wall below brightens, very slightly. That afternoon, in that courtyard, a magistrate who had been about to sign a bought verdict looks up at the wall, and puts down the brush.

choices.text: Watch, and leave it be

effects.log: You watch the faded beast on the wall below for a long time. It is enough, you think, that it is there. The ones who need to see it, see it. It does not need to be bright to be looking.

events.text: You have been called before heaven's tribunal. Not as the accused: as a witness, in the matter of {npc}, an envoy of the Jade court who is accused of selling a drought to a kingdom below. The hall is of white cloud and jade, the judge's seat too bright to look at, and at its foot, white as a candle, lies a beast with one horn. You have seen its likeness, painted on a hundred walls far below. {npc} smiles at you warmly across the hall, as if you were old friends.

choices.text: Give your testimony plainly

effects.log: You say what you saw: the envoy's cloud over the kingdom, the rain held back, the gold that went up. No more. {npc} smiles through all of it. At the foot of the seat the beast lifts its head and looks at {npc}, and {npc}'s smile, for the first time, falters.

choices.text: Watch the beast, not the envoy

ok.log: You watch the beast while {npc} speaks, and see what nobody else in the hall sees: every time {npc} says the word 'mercy', the beast's ears move. You say so, when it is your turn. The judge's light turns toward {npc}, and {npc} stops smiling for good.

fail.log: You watch the beast and cannot read it; it is older than anything you know how to read. You give your testimony plainly in the end, and that is enough.

events.text: {npc}, the envoy of the Jade court, comes to your palace of cloud after the tribunal, still smiling, though the verdict went against {npc}. "No hard feelings," {npc} says. "Let me make you a gift: a seat on the Jade council. It only needs one small thing: that you say, if anyone asks, that the beast at the judge's feet is growing old, and sees less than it did."

choices.text: Refuse to the envoy's face

effects.log: "It sees exactly as much as it did," you say. "Which is why you are here." {npc} goes on smiling, and goes. You never get a seat on the Jade council. You find you do not miss it.

choices.text: Ask the beast what to say

effects.log: You go to the tribunal and ask it. The beast looks at you, and then turns its head and looks at the door of your palace, where {npc} is waiting. Its ears go up. That is all. You go back and tell {npc} that you have been answered. {npc} stops smiling.

choices.text: Accept, and say it once, quietly

effects.log: You take the seat. Once, when someone asks, you say the beast is growing old. You do not say it again. You never need to. The next time you pass the tribunal, the beast at the foot of the seat lifts its head and looks at you for a long moment, and that is the whole of your punishment, and it is enough.

events.text: Among the heavenly immortals who sit in the gallery of the tribunal there is one you have noticed, quiet, with scarred hands, who never misses a hearing. At last you ask. "I was a slave once," the immortal says. "In a capital below. I beat the petition drum with my bare hands at night, and the only one awake to hear it was a beast under the tower. It sits up there now. I come to watch it work."

choices.text: Sit and watch with them

effects.log: You sit beside the immortal with scarred hands through a whole season of hearings. Neither of you says much. Once, at the end of a hard case, the beast at the judge's feet turns its head toward the gallery and lays its ears back, and the immortal beside you weeps without a sound.

choices.text: Ask what happened after the drum

effects.log: "I was heard," the immortal says simply. "The master who killed my brother was punished. I was freed. I lived a long life and cultivated, and here I am." The immortal looks at their hands. "I keep the scars. They are the only thing I own that the drum gave me."

events.text: The Divine Ram asks for you. It is no longer a beast that sees the truth, they say in the Upper Realm; it is the truth, and where it stands no lie can be spoken aloud. Its hall is white and silent. Emperors have come out of it unable to speak for a year. It asks you, a sovereign, for one sentence: whatever you like, in its hall, aloud.

choices.text: Say the truest thing you know

effects.log: You stand in the white hall and say it. It is a short sentence about something you have never said even to yourself. It comes out easily, like breathing out. The Divine Ram lays its ears back, and the hall rings very softly, like a struck bowl, for a long time after.

choices.text: Try to say something kind that is not quite true

effects.log: You open your mouth to say a kind small lie, the kind you have said ten thousand times, and it is not there. The words are simply gone, like a step that is not where your foot expected. You stand in silence. Then you say the true one, which is less kind and better. The Ram's ears go back.

choices.text: Say nothing at all

effects.log: You stand in the white hall and say nothing. The silence is the truest thing you have ever made. After a very long time the Divine Ram lays its ears back, and you understand that silence was a sentence too, and that it was heard.

events.text: {npc}, a sovereign of a neighbouring heaven, comes to you with a request. {npc} wants a hall like the Divine Ram's: a hall where no lie can be spoken. "Only mine," {npc} adds. "Where only my truth can be spoken." {npc} thinks you, who spoke in the Ram's hall, might know how it is built.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that such a hall would be a prison

effects.log: "A hall where only your truth can be spoken," you say, "is a hall where every other truth is a lie. That is not the Ram's hall. That is a cage." {npc} goes away angry. A thousand years later {npc} comes back and thanks you, which is quick, for a sovereign.

choices.text: Take {npc} to the Ram's hall

effects.log: You take {npc} to the white hall. {npc} opens {his} mouth to speak and finds nothing there but the truth, and it is not the one {npc} came to say. {npc} stands silent a long time and then leaves without a word, and does not build a hall.

events.text: An envoy of some court of heaven finds you on a terrace of cloud with a sealed scroll and a warm smile. "A small matter," {npc} says. "Your signature as a witness that this treaty was freely agreed. Everyone else has signed." {npc} is smiling very warmly. Somewhere far off in the mist, very faint, there is a white glow and the sound of a bell.

choices.text: Read every word before signing

effects.log: It takes a day. {npc} smiles through all of it, a little less each hour. On the last page, in very small characters, the treaty gives one heaven's rain to another for ten thousand years. You do not sign. The bell in the mist stops ringing.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether it was freely agreed

effects.log: "Of course," {npc} says. Far off in the mist the bell rings, once, sharp. {npc} hears it too. The smile goes thin. "Mostly," {npc} says. You hand the scroll back unsigned.

choices.text: Sign: it is a small matter

effects.log: You sign. {npc} thanks you warmly. The bell in the mist rings for three days. Ten years later you learn what the treaty was, and why the bell rang, and you go to the court of debts and ask how to unsign a thing.

events.text: In the night you wake to a bell: one note, far off, clear, from the direction of the capital, though the capital is days away. You have heard it before, since you met the beast. It rings when there is a fire, people say, and when someone lies who should not.

choices.text: Get up and check every lamp in the house

effects.log: Every lamp, every brazier, the kitchen fire. In the kitchen a coal has rolled from the hearth onto the straw mat and is smouldering. You put it out with a dipper of water and stand in the dark kitchen with your heart going. Far off, the bell does not ring again.

choices.text: Lie still and think whether you lied today

effects.log: You lie still and go through your day. There it is: a small one, to a neighbour, about a borrowed sieve. In the morning you take the sieve back. The bell, you suspect, was not about you at all. It does not matter. The sieve needed returning.

events.text: A chinaberry leaf on your doorstep at dawn, fresh, bitter-smelling, with no chinaberry tree for a mile. The old people say it is left at the door of someone who is about to be asked to tell the truth.

choices.text: Chew it, for the bitterness

effects.log: Bitter as the back of a tongue. It clears your head the way cold water does. That afternoon someone asks you a question you would rather not answer, and you answer it truly, and find that the bitterness was the worst part.

choices.text: Put it in a bowl of water by the door

effects.log: It stays green in the bowl for a month. Visitors look at it and, for some reason, tell you things they had not meant to. You learn a great deal that month.

events.text: You are a labourer on the city works, and the work this spring is strange: digging out the old pond before the South Gate, which a minister had filled in ten years ago to build a storehouse. The storehouse has been pulled down. The old foreman says the pond was dug when the city was founded to face the fire mountain in the south: the gate's name plaque hung upright like a flame, the pond before it, and the stone beasts at the palace. "Three guards," the foreman says. "The minister took one away to keep his rice dry. Two of his own houses burned."
events.arc: The Pond at the South Gate

choices.text: Dig hard: the city needs its pond

effects.log: You dig through the summer. When the water comes back into the old pond, clear from a spring under the gate, the foreman throws in a handful of rice and says a few words to the south. That year the capital has no fire worth the name, and the foreman takes all the credit, loudly, at every tavern.

choices.text: Ask the foreman whether he believes it

effects.log: "Believe?" the foreman says. "I have dug this pond twice and filled it once. When it was full, the city burned less. When it was empty, it burned more. I do not need to believe. I can count."

events.text: Years after the pond was dug out, a new minister proposes filling it in again: the land is valuable, the superstition old-fashioned. A petition is going round the ward against it. You dug that pond.
events.arc: The Pond at the South Gate

choices.text: Sign the petition and say why

effects.log: You sign, and add a line under your name: I dug it, and I counted the fires. The petition goes to the court with your line in it. The pond stays. The minister builds the storehouse somewhere else, where it burns down within the year, as the foreman would have said it would.

choices.text: Stay out of the matter

effects.log: You stay out of it. The pond is filled. You walk past the dry square of earth before the South Gate on summer evenings and feel the heat coming off it, and remember the clear water, and are sorry.

events.text: A shaman has come to the village with bells and a fan and a bowl of water in which, the shaman says, the spirits show who brought the sickness on the headman's house. The bowl, after much dancing, shows the face of the poorest widow in the village, who has no family to speak for her. The village is muttering. You were at the back of the yard, and you saw the shaman's assistant drop something into the water.

choices.text: Say what you saw, in front of everyone

ok.log: You say it loud. The assistant drops the second packet. The headman, who is not a fool, has the shaman out of the village by dawn, and sends rice to the widow. The bowl of water is left behind on the low table, and in the morning there is a single chinaberry leaf floating in it.

fail.log: Nobody listens to you, and the shaman's assistant cuffs you for interrupting a rite. But you go to the widow's house that night and sit with her by the door with a stick, and nobody comes. In the morning the shaman is gone. (-5 health)

choices.text: Take the widow's side quietly, and stay with her

effects.log: You walk the widow home and sit at her gate all night. Nobody comes. In the morning the shaman has left, and the headman's house is still sick, and somebody, at last, thinks to look at the headman's well.

events.text: Another shaman comes to the village, an old one, tired, with no assistant. At the bedside of a dying woman the shaman tells her that her son, lost at sea ten years ago, is waiting for her on the other side, well and happy. Nobody knows if it is true. The shaman sees you watching from the door, and holds your eyes, and waits.

choices.text: Say nothing: let her die comforted

effects.log: You say nothing. The woman dies smiling. Afterwards, in the yard, the old shaman says to you: "I do not know if it was true. I know it was kind. The horned one would butt me for it." A pause. "I think it would butt me gently."

choices.text: Ask the shaman afterward whether it was true

effects.log: "I do not know," the shaman says. "I never know. I say what the dying need. The young one I hear you threw out of the village said what the living wanted. That is the difference between us." You think about that for a long time.

events.text: The king sends for you in private, at night, and gives you a list of names: ministers, scholars, a cousin. "These are my enemies," the king says. "You are the only person in the kingdom strong enough to bring the beast before the gate into my council hall. Bring it. Let it look at them. If it lowers its horn, I will know." The list is in the king's own hand. Some of the names are honest people.

choices.text: Agree, on one condition: the king stands in the line too

effects.log: The king stares at you. Then, slowly, laughs. "You think I am afraid of it." You say nothing. The list goes into the candle flame, and the king says, still laughing, that you are either the most loyal subject in the kingdom or the least. You both know which.

choices.text: Refuse outright

effects.log: "It is not a dog," you say. "And I am not a leash." You spend a season under house arrest for it. At the end of the season the king's cousin, one of the names, is found to be honest after all, and you are released without a word. (-10 health)

choices.text: Bring it the list, not the ministers

ok.log: You take the list to the gate and hold it up before the beast. It looks at the paper for a long time. Then it lowers its horn, very gently, at the list itself, at the hand that wrote it. You carry the list back to the king and tell him what it did. The king does not ask for the beast again.

fail.log: The beast will not look at the list at all; it turns its head away. You cannot tell the king what that means, because you do not know. The king takes it as a refusal, and you as a fool, and both of you are a little right.

events.text: Your teacher told you, when you left the training hall, that you were let go because the hall had nothing more to teach you. Lately, from a drunk old disciple of the same hall, you have heard another story: that your place was sold. You have walked for a month with that in your chest. Tonight, at a spring in the hills, a beast with scales and one horn is drinking on the far bank, and the travellers' tales say it knows a lie when it hears one.

choices.text: Say your teacher's words aloud, and watch it

effects.log: You say it across the water, word for word as your teacher said it. The beast lifts its dripping head and listens. Its ears do not go up. They go back, slowly, flat. Your teacher did not lie. You sit by the spring until the stars are out, with the drunk disciple's story going out of you like a fever breaking.

choices.text: Say the drunk disciple's story aloud instead

effects.log: You say the other story. The beast's ears go up and stay up, and it looks at you a long time, and goes back to drinking. Whatever the drunk disciple thought, it was not true. You feel foolish, and then, all at once, enormously relieved.

choices.text: Ask it nothing: some answers are your own to find

effects.log: You ask nothing. You go back to the training hall instead, a month's walk, and ask your teacher straight. Your teacher tells you the whole story, which is longer and sadder than either version, and true. You are glad you heard it from a person.

events.text: Years later, a young swordsman of your own training comes to you with a story heard from a drunk: that you lied to them about something that matters. They are standing in your yard with their hands shaking.

choices.text: Tell them the whole truth, longer and sadder

effects.log: You tell them all of it, the way your own teacher once told you. It takes until midnight. At the end they are crying and so are you, and nothing is broken that was not already broken, and something is mended.

choices.text: Send them to the spring in the hills

effects.log: "Go and say what I told you to the beast at the spring," you say. They go. They come back a month later and bow to you without a word, and never mention the drunk again.

events.text: {npc}, a martial master as famous as you and a great deal angrier, has beaten the petition drum against you, swearing before the court that you poisoned {his} disciple in a duel. You did not. The court is full. And at the foot of the drum tower lies the beast with one horn, which has not taken its eyes off {npc} since the drum stopped.

choices.text: Ask the court to let the beast choose

effects.log: The court agrees. The beast stands, walks the length of the court, and lowers its horn at {npc}. The old law is plain: a false accuser takes the punishment the accused would have had. {npc} goes white and then red, and draws, there in the court, and the guards close in.

choices.text: Answer every charge, calmly, point by point

ok.log: Point by point: the duel, the cup, the physician. By the end the court does not need the beast, though it lays its ears back at you as you sit down. {npc} is found a false accuser, and by the old law must suffer what {npc} sought for you.

fail.log: You lose your thread under {npc}'s shouting, and for a terrible hour the court leans toward the charge. Then the beast stands and lowers its horn at {npc}, and the court turns like a boat in the current. (-8 health)

events.text: By the old law {npc}, the master who accused you falsely, must suffer the punishment {npc} sought for you: exile to a far island. {npc} will not accept it. The guards say no one in the capital is strong enough to make {npc} go, except, perhaps, you. The court asks whether you will plead for mercy, or carry out the sentence.

choices.text: Plead for the sentence to be lightened

effects.log: You plead, and the court, astonished, cuts the exile to five years. {npc} goes, of {his} own accord, without a fight. Five years later {npc} comes back and stands at your gate, and does not say thank you, and does not need to.

choices.text: Escort {npc} to the island yourself

ok.log: {npc} fights you at the river crossing, as you knew {npc} would, and loses, as you knew {npc} would. The rest of the journey is silent. At the island {npc} turns and says one true sentence: that the disciple died of {his} own reckless training. You take that back to the disciple's family.

fail.log: {npc} fights you at the river crossing and wins, and escapes into the hills. But the beast before the gate, they say, turned its head that night toward the hills and kept it turned for a year, and {npc} was never seen in any town again. (-20 health)

choices.text: Leave it to the court

effects.log: You leave it to the court. The court, having no one strong enough, quietly lets {npc} leave the capital instead. It is not justice. It is not nothing.

events.text: You are the hired escort of a minister newly risen and very proud. Before the palace gate, where the great beast with one horn lies facing south, every official dismounts and walks; it is the custom. Your minister does not. "A stone animal," the minister says loudly, and rides on toward the gate. The beast's head turns.

choices.text: Take the bridle and stop the horse

ok.log: You take the bridle and the horse stops, and the minister, furious, must either get down or be seen arguing with an escort in front of the whole gate. The minister gets down. The beast's head turns back to the south. You are dismissed that evening, and hired the next week by a minister who heard about it, and who walks.

fail.log: The minister lashes you across the hand with a riding whip and rides on. Three paces from the gate the horse stops dead, by itself, and will not go on, and the minister has to get down after all in front of everyone. (-6 health)

choices.text: Warn the minister quietly

effects.log: "The ones who ride past it," you say, low, "are the ones it remembers." The minister laughs, and then glances at the beast, and the beast is looking straight back. The minister gets down, slowly, as if it had been the plan all along.

choices.text: Let the minister ride on: not your business

effects.log: You let the minister ride. Nothing happens. Nothing at all, for three years. Then the minister is impeached by the inspectors' office for a long list of things, and you remember the way the beast's head turned, and how long it watched.

events.text: You are in a magistrate's courtyard on some small business, and on the wall behind the porch is an old faded painting of a judge and a beast with one horn. Everyone else ignores it. You cannot stop looking at it, because its painted eye, alone of all the faded paint, is bright and wet, and it is looking at you as if it has been waiting for you to come in.

choices.text: Look back at it, steadily

effects.log: You look back. For a long moment you are not in the courtyard at all: you are lying at the foot of a seat too bright to look at, and every painted courtyard under heaven is a window, and you can see through all of them at once. Then you are only yourself, with your papers, blinking. The clerk asks if you are unwell.

choices.text: Bow to it, as to an elder

effects.log: You bow, absurdly, to a painting. The painted ears, very slightly, flatten. The magistrate, who saw, decides your small business in your favour without quite knowing why.

events.text: A case in the magistrate's courtyard where the painted beast looked at you: a widow and a merchant, a debt and a forged seal. The magistrate is lost. You find you know, as plainly as you know your own name, which of them is lying, and you have no way to prove it.

choices.text: Ask the magistrate to look at the painting while they speak

ok.log: The magistrate humours you. The merchant speaks, and the painted beast's eye, bright on the faded wall, turns, plainly, toward the merchant. The whole courtyard sees it. The merchant confesses on the spot. You go home and sit in your yard for a long time, shaking, with the feeling of having been, for a moment, very old.

fail.log: The magistrate refuses to be ordered about by a commoner. But that night the magistrate dreams of the painting, and in the morning reopens the case and finds the forged seal. You hear about it at the well.

choices.text: Say nothing: you cannot prove it

effects.log: You say nothing. The case goes the wrong way. Walking out, you glance at the painting, and its eye is still on you, and it does not seem angry: only patient, the way a judge is patient with a witness who has not yet learned to speak.

events.text: In heaven's tribunal, as a visitor, you come to the foot of the judgement seat. The beast that lies there, white as a candle, lifts its head as you approach, and lays its ears back, and makes room beside it on the step, as if for someone who used to sit there.

choices.text: Sit beside it, for one hearing

effects.log: You sit on the step beside it through one hearing, and see the court as it sees it: every mouth and every heart, and where they are the same shape and where they are not. It is too much and it is beautiful. When you stand, the step is warm.

choices.text: Bow, and leave the place empty

effects.log: You bow and do not sit. The beast's ears stay back a long while. A seat you once filled, you think, should be left for whoever fills it now.

events.text: You have noticed it since you were small: you cannot lie aloud. Not out of virtue. You open your mouth to tell the simplest lie, that you have done your chores, that you like the soup, and the words are simply not there, like a step missing in the dark. You can stay silent. You cannot say what is not.

choices.text: Learn to live with it, and choose your silences

effects.log: You learn the art of the true thing said kindly, and the art of silence. It takes years. By the time you are grown, people come to you from three villages away to hear an answer they can trust, and you have become very good at saying, gently, "I would rather not say."

choices.text: Fight it: practise lying in secret

effects.log: You practise alone in the woodshed, a lie a day. Nothing comes. Once, after a month, you manage half a lie before the words fail, and it tastes so strange and sour in your mouth that you never try again.

events.text: Bandits have taken the village, and their leader holds a knife to the headman's grandson and asks you where the village has hidden its seed rice. Everyone knows you cannot lie. Everyone is looking at you.

choices.text: Say nothing at all

effects.log: You say nothing. The leader strikes you, again and again, and you say nothing. In the end, unnerved by a silence that will not break, the bandits take what they can carry and go, and leave the boy. The seed rice stays hidden. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell the truth, in a way that helps

ok.log: "It is under the shrine of the mountain god," you say, which is true, "and the mountain god does not forgive thieves," which is also, as it happens, true. The bandits know the stories about that shrine. They let the boy go and leave by the valley road, and do not come back.

fail.log: You try to find a true thing that helps and the words tangle, and the leader loses patience and takes half the seed rice. But only half: you had, without meaning to, told the truth about the smaller store. (-8 health)

events.text: The first time you see the capital you walk straight to the palace gate as if you had an appointment, and stop between the two stone beasts that guard it, one on each side, faces turned south toward the mountain shaped like flame. You put your hand on the nearer one. It is warm. And the small bronze bell at its throat, which the gate guards say has not rung in your lifetime, rings once.

choices.text: Put your other hand on the other one

effects.log: Both bells ring together, once. The gate guards stare. You stand between the two stone beasts with a hand on each and feel, very far off, a clear cold spring at the edge of the world, and someone beside you there who was always beside you. Then you are only a traveller, with your hands on two warm stones.

choices.text: Look south, the way they look

effects.log: You turn and look south with them, at the flame-shaped mountain across the river. You know its every ridge. You know where the sparks come from in a dry spring with the wind from the northwest. You know, and you do not know how you know, that the city behind you has not burned in a long time.

events.text: In the night, in the capital, the bells of the stone pair before the gate begin to ring together, and do not stop. You are out of bed before you know why. Somewhere in the lanes south of the palace, there is a smell of smoke.

choices.text: Run toward the smoke

ok.log: You run to the smoke and find it: a lamp gone over in a paper-maker's shed, the paper just catching. You have it out with a rain barrel before the shed is half gone. When you walk back past the gate at dawn the bells are silent, and the stone beasts' ears, you would swear, are back.

fail.log: You get there as the fire takes the shed, and you are burned dragging the paper-maker out. But the neighbours, woken by the bells, come running with buckets, and the fire goes no further than the shed. (-10 health)

choices.text: Run to the gate and ask them where

effects.log: You stand between the stone pair, out of breath, and ask aloud. Both stone heads face south. But the bells ring louder as you turn east, and you run east, and find the fire in a dyer's yard, and raise the lane. By dawn it is out.

events.text: Learning your characters, you noticed something the village schoolmaster never had: in the law books, some laws are written crooked. Not the brushwork. The characters themselves lean, very slightly, as if something inside them were pushing to get out. And the old character for law itself, when you write it, always comes out with a small shape in the middle of it that looks like a beast with one horn.

choices.text: Make a list of the crooked laws

effects.log: A list, over years. When you check them, every crooked law turns out to have been written for one person's benefit and dressed up as for everyone's: a tax that falls only on one county, a rule about wells that one family wrote. The straight laws are dull. You come to love the dull ones.

choices.text: Ask the village schoolmaster about the shape in the character

effects.log: The old schoolmaster looks at your character for law for a long time and then says that, in the oldest form of it, there was a beast inside: water, which finds its level, and the beast that knew right from wrong, and the stroke that drives out. "Nobody writes it that way now," the schoolmaster says. "Except you, it seems."

events.text: The court has published a new law, and it is posted on the wall of the county office. Everyone reads it as fair. To you, from across the street, it is so crooked the characters are almost falling off the paper.

choices.text: Find out who it was written for

ok.log: It takes a season of reading land registers. The law, which forbids new mills on the river, was written for the one family that already owns the mill. You send your findings to the inspectors' office, and the law is quietly withdrawn. On the wall, the next notice is written perfectly straight.

fail.log: You cannot find it in the registers. But you know. Every time you pass the notice it leans further, and a year later it is withdrawn after someone else finds what you could not.

choices.text: Tell nobody: who would believe crooked characters

effects.log: You tell nobody. But you never once obey that law in your heart, and you notice that the mill it protects burns down in a dry spring, and that nobody can say how the fire started.

events.text: A pawnbroker's widow is selling up, and among the junk in a lacquer box is an old official's chest badge, a beast with one horn in white and gold silk, its eye a single knot of white thread. She wants a copper for it. When you pick it up, the room goes clearer, the way a room does when a window is washed.

choices.text: Buy it

effects.log: One copper. You carry it home inside your coat. That evening at supper a friend tells a story about a lost purse, and the badge against your chest goes cold as well water, and you look at the friend, and the friend goes red and changes the subject. You keep the badge all your life. It never once warms for a lie.

choices.text: Ask her where it came from

effects.log: "An old inspector pawned it," she says, "forty years ago, and never came back. They said there was a sliver of something in every badge of that office once, from a beast that gave its sight away. Most of them wore out." She looks at it. "That one did not." She gives it to you for nothing.

events.text: You have worn the old badge under your coat for years, and it has never failed you: cold for a lie, quiet for the truth. Today, at the magistrate's court, a young junior inspector is trying a case alone, badly, and you can feel the badge going cold and cold as the witnesses lie to the inspector's face.

choices.text: Give the badge to the young inspector

effects.log: After the court rises you find the young inspector in the yard, near tears, and press the badge into their hand without explaining. A week later the same court, the same witnesses: the inspector stops in the middle of a question, puts a hand to the chest, and turns slowly to look at the liar. You walk home lighter. A sliver of sight is meant to be passed on.

choices.text: Stand up and point out the liars yourself

ok.log: You stand and name them, one by one, and the young inspector, startled, checks each of them and finds you right. Afterward the inspector asks how you knew. You show the badge under your coat. The inspector stares at it a long time.

fail.log: You stand and are thrown out of the court for interrupting. But the young inspector saw your face, and asks the witnesses the same questions again, more slowly, and catches two of them. (-6 health)

events.text: On a dare you climb the mountain shaped like flame, south of the capital, in the dry season. At the summit, on the bare rock, there is a small pool of water, clear and cold, that the old people say has never once dried in three hundred years, not in the worst drought. You kneel beside it. You know how deep it is without looking. You know how it got there.

choices.text: Drink from it

effects.log: The water is cold all the way down, and tastes of nothing and of smoke at once. In your chest, for a moment, there is a great heat being held, and held, and held, and then a vast relief. You sit on the summit until the sun goes down over the capital, which has not burned in your lifetime.

choices.text: Wash your face in it

effects.log: You wash your face and look at your reflection, and for a moment it is not your face at all: scales, a curly mane, one horn, and a mouth full of fire, closed. Then it is you, with wet cheeks. You climb down very slowly.

events.text: A drought so bad that the wells of the capital are dry, and the river is a ditch. Somebody remembers the pool on the summit of the fire mountain, and the court sends men with jars to empty it into the palace cisterns. You are among those sent, and you know what is under that water.

choices.text: Tell the court the pool must not be emptied

ok.log: You tell them, and somehow they listen: the pool is the lid on the mountain's fire. The jars come back empty. The capital digs new wells and lives through the drought, and the mountain stays quiet.

fail.log: Nobody listens. You stand at the summit and refuse to let them dip their jars, and are beaten for it. But while they are beating you the sky clouds over, and it rains for the first time in a year, and the jars are left on the summit, empty. (-8 health)

choices.text: Fill your own jar, and only one

effects.log: One jar, carried down to an old person's house in the poorest ward. The pool on the summit, when you look back from the ridge, has not gone down by a finger. You think: it never would have gone down for one jar of kindness. Only for greed.

events.text: Your eyes are a little too clear. Everyone says so: the midwife, the neighbours, the village teacher. When someone lies to you, even kindly, you look at them, and keep looking, and they stop. It is not something you do on purpose. It is only that your eyes do not seem to know how to believe a thing that is not so. People call it, half joking, the haechi's eye.

choices.text: Learn to look away when it would be kind

effects.log: You learn it slowly: when an elder says the pain is nothing, you look away. When a friend says they are fine, you look away and stay nearby. The haechi's eye, you learn, is not only for catching. It is also for knowing when to close.

choices.text: Keep looking, always

effects.log: You keep looking. It makes you few friends and no enemies who stay. By the time you are grown, every lie in the village is told when you are out of the room, and you are asked to witness every contract.

events.text: The examination hall. You have sat the civil examination, and passed, and the court offers you a post in the inspectors' office, with the black hat and the one-horned beast stitched on the front. When the hat is set on your head, it fits as if it had been made for you. It feels, oddly, like putting on an old coat.

choices.text: Take the post, and make one vow

effects.log: You take it, and vow, in your own head, not aloud, never to tell a lie while you wear it. It is the easiest vow you have ever made. You keep it for years, and the hat never once has to hang on its peg.

choices.text: Refuse: one life in that hat was enough

effects.log: You take the hat off and hand it back, and the examiners are scandalised. You cannot explain. You only know, as surely as you know your name, that you have worn this hat before for a whole life, and that it was good, and that this life is for something else.

events.text: The kingdom has a day of great joy: a war ended, or a famine broken, or a good king crowned, and the whole capital is in the streets. An old brewer's grandchild remembers a story: jars of white wine buried a hundred years ago beneath the stone beasts before the palace gate, to be opened on a day the whole land is glad. They are digging them up. You are in the crowd, and you know, as plainly as your own name, exactly where the jars are.

choices.text: Show them where to dig

effects.log: "There," you say, "under the left forefoot, three jars, and one more behind, smaller." They dig, and there they are. The first jar is opened and the wine is clear and old and smells of a hundred years of waiting. They give you the first cup, because you knew. It tastes like having been right to wait.

choices.text: Say nothing, and watch them find it

effects.log: You watch them search for an hour and find it on their own. That is better, you think. The wine is shared out by the cup to everyone in the crowd. When your cup comes you hold it and pass it on to the old man behind you, standing beside the stone beast, and you could swear its stone flank is warm against your arm.

events.text: The brewer's grandchild, who dug up the old jars, comes to you afterward: they want to bury new ones, for another hundred years, for the next good day. They ask you, who knew where the old ones were, to choose the place.

choices.text: Choose the same place, beneath the stone feet

effects.log: Under the same stone forefoot, three jars and a little one. You tamp the earth down yourself. You will not be alive to drink it. You find that does not matter at all: the waiting is the gift.

choices.text: Say: let the next generation choose

effects.log: "Let them choose," you say. "A good year is not something we can decide for them." The grandchild buries the jars anyway, somewhere, and never tells you where. That, you think, is right.

events.text: Wherever you go, you cannot pass a jar of standing water without looking in. In the palace, where you have some small business, there are great bronze jars at the corners of every hall, kept full against the fire demon. Looking into one at night, you see, behind your own reflection, under the water, a beast with one horn lying curled at the bottom of the jar, looking up.

choices.text: Keep the jars full yourself, every night

effects.log: You take it on, unasked: every jar, every night, to the brim. The water carriers think you are mad. You know whose bed it is.

choices.text: Speak to it

effects.log: "Is it you?" you ask the water. The beast at the bottom of the jar lays its ears back. The surface goes so still that you can see every star in it. You understand that you are talking to yourself, a long time ago, and that you are, somehow, being reassured.

events.text: A dry night in the palace, and you are at the jar by the throne hall when something red comes over the wall, like a person made of coals, and bends over the water to see whether it is safe to go in. It sees its own face. You see it see.

choices.text: Hold up a lantern so it sees itself clearly

effects.log: You lift your lantern over the jar. The face in the water is lit, every crack and ember of it, and the demon gives a soundless scream and goes back over the wall in a rush of heat. Under the water, a horned shape turns over, contented, and settles.

choices.text: Speak to the demon, not the jar

ok.log: "It is only your face," you say to it. "That is all it has ever been." The demon looks at you, and back at the water, and for a long moment does not run. Then it goes, slowly, over the wall, and the jar is quiet. You do not know if you have done a kindness or a foolishness. Perhaps both.

fail.log: You speak and it turns from the jar to you, and the heat of its looking blisters your cheek, and then it sees itself again in the water over your shoulder, and flees. (-8 health)

events.text: You have come north, to the frontier, for reasons you could not explain to anyone: a pull, like a smell of birch and snow. Out here the trappers and the soldiers and the salt smugglers say there are no quarrels that last. Disputes settle themselves at the springs. And at a clear spring in the birches, at dawn, you see two small beasts with scales and horns like white candle-buds playing in the water.

choices.text: Stay hidden and watch them

effects.log: You watch until the sun is high. They butt each other over nothing, the way kids do, and fall in the spring, and climb out shaking water off their scales. You know, without knowing how, that their grandmother lies somewhere near, very old, and that you used to be the one they would have run to.

choices.text: Step out and let them see you

effects.log: You step out. Both small heads come up. Then both small beasts lay their ears back flat and bow, clumsily, the way they must have been taught to bow to the upright, and run off into the birches. You stand by the spring a long time with your eyes stinging.

events.text: On the frontier, two trapper camps are about to fight over a line of sable traps, knives out, and you are between them. Nobody here knows you. But both camps, you notice, keep glancing toward the spring in the birches behind you, where something with a white horn is drinking.

choices.text: Suggest they take it to the spring

effects.log: "Ask at the spring," you say, and both camps go quiet, as if you had said something holy. They walk to the spring together, and the beast lifts its head, and looks at one trapper, and that trapper puts away the knife and admits to moving the traps. Nobody bleeds. It is, the old trappers say, how things are done here.

choices.text: Settle it yourself before anyone reaches the spring

ok.log: You make them each tell it from the start, slowly, and halfway through, one of them stops and laughs and admits it. The beast at the spring lifts its head and lays its ears back toward you. You feel, absurdly, that you have been praised by family.

fail.log: Someone takes a swing at you. But the noise brings the beast up from the spring, and at the sight of it every knife goes away, and the quarrel ends without another word. (-6 health)

events.text: Before the palace gate there is a pair of stone lions with scales and curly manes and smooth brows, and you hate them. You do not know why. Every time you pass, you look at the smooth place on the forehead of the left one and your own forehead aches, as if something had been broken off there.

choices.text: Ask an old carver why the brows are smooth

effects.log: "They always were," the old carver says. Then, slowly: "My grandmaster said there used to be a horn, in the old pictures. Nobody remembers why it was left off. We forgot it was ever there." You walk away with your forehead aching, and that night you dream of a sound like a bowl breaking.

choices.text: Touch the smooth brow

effects.log: Cold stone, smooth as a river pebble. And for a moment you see nothing at all, the way it sees nothing: no truth, no lie, only stone and grey sky. You take your hand away and the world comes back, full of liars and honest people, and you are, for once, glad of all of them. (-3 health)

events.text: The stone lions before the gate are to be repaired, and the work has gone to a carver's yard where you work, or near which you live, or where you happen to be passing with a chisel in your hands and more skill than you can explain. The overseer says: smooth the brows again, as they were.

choices.text: Carve a small horn back into the left one at night

ok.log: By lantern light, a small horn, sloping back from the brow like a candle flame bent by the wind. In the morning the overseer is furious, and then, looking at it, is not. It stays. The ache in your own forehead is gone for the rest of your life.

fail.log: Your hand slips and the horn comes out a lump. The overseer has it smoothed away. But you keep the chip of stone that fell, and your forehead aches a little less.

choices.text: Smooth it, as ordered: it is only stone now

effects.log: You smooth it. It is only stone. Whatever saw through that brow saw its last a long time ago, and grieving for it will not make it see. You go home and sleep, for once, without the dream of the breaking bowl.

events.text: In an archive, or a scholar's family chest, or a junk stall, you come across an old royal warrant from one of the great purges of the scholars, with a list of names, and stamped at the top in faded red, the image of a beast with one horn. Your hands start shaking before you have read a word. You know every one of the names.

choices.text: Read the names aloud, one by one

effects.log: You read them all, slowly, in the quiet room. Forty-one names. At each one there is a face in your head, and the moment a horn was lowered at it because a throne pointed. When you finish you are weeping, and you do not know for whom: for them, or for the beast that was bought.

choices.text: Burn it

effects.log: You burn it in the brazier. The red beast curls and blackens. It does not help. The names stay in your head, every one, and you understand that burning a thing does not unmake it, and that the only way out of a lie is through the truth.

events.text: A descendant of one of the scholars on the old warrant lives in your town, poor, a teacher of village children, the family ruined by a horn that was lowered at the wrong person three hundred years ago. You have found out who. You do not know what you owe them. You only know you owe it.

choices.text: Go to them and tell them the truth of the warrant

effects.log: You tell them all of it: the purge, the beast, the throne that pointed. You do not say how you know. The teacher listens and says: "My family always said great-grandfather was innocent. Nobody believed us." You say you do. It is a small thing to give. It is more than they have ever been given.

choices.text: Help the family quietly, for the rest of your life (20 taels)

effects.log: Twenty taels, and then more, quietly, every year, for the schoolhouse roof and the teacher's children's schooling. They never know why. You never tell. It is not a mending. It is all you have.

choices.text: Stay away: some debts cannot be paid

effects.log: You stay away. But you find yourself, once a year, walking past the schoolhouse and stopping to listen to the children reciting, and the sound of them is like a bell that will not stop ringing.

events.text: Behind the palace, by a wall where nobody goes, there is a great lump wrapped in rotten straw mats and tied with rope, left there so long that grass grows on it. Everybody says it is old building stone. You cannot pass it without your chest going tight, as if you were the one tied up, and the city were burning on the other side of the wall.

choices.text: Untie the ropes and pull back the straw

effects.log: Underneath, a stone beast with scales and a curly mane and one horn, its face turned to the wall. You stand there in the snow with the rotten straw in your hands. That winter, for the first time in years, there is no great fire in the city, and nobody connects the two things but you.

choices.text: Ask the palace gardener what it is

effects.log: "One of the gate beasts," the gardener says. "From before. A court that did not believe in them had them moved out of the way, and wrapped, and forgotten. The city burned that winter. People blamed the moving." The gardener looks at the lump of straw. "I sweep round it. I do not know why."

events.text: You have petitioned for the stone beast behind the palace to be set back before the gate, and the court is hearing it. A young official laughs: a superstition, a stone animal, and the city has a fire office now. Another official, older, is listening very carefully.

choices.text: Say only: the city burned when it was moved

ok.log: "The city burned when it was moved," you say, "and burns less when it is looked after. I do not ask you to believe. I ask you to count." The older official counts. The beast goes back before the gate that spring, faces south, and the young official, to his credit, comes to watch it set down.

fail.log: They laugh you out of the hall. But the older official comes to see the straw-wrapped stone behind the palace that evening, alone, and stands in front of it a long time, and has it moved, quietly, to a sheltered spot, unwrapped, with its face to the south. It is a start.

choices.text: Withdraw the petition and look after it yourself

effects.log: You withdraw it. Instead, every winter, you go behind the palace and brush the snow off the stone beast and turn its face, a little at a time, toward the south. It takes years. When at last it faces the mountain, there is a winter without a single fire.

events.text: In a back room of a great sect's treasury, or a rich merchant's strong room, or a dark apothecary, you are shown a small silver box of grey powder: Haechi Horn Powder, they say, real, from a beast hunted for its horn long ago. Priceless. A pinch shows a drinker every lie. Everyone who has taken it has died seeing enemies at every table. When the box is opened you feel sick, and your own forehead throbs, and you know, beyond any doubt, whose horn it was.

choices.text: Buy it, whatever it costs, and bury it

effects.log: Thirty taels, every coin you have and some borrowed. You carry the box north for a month to a clear spring at the edge of the birch forests, and pour the powder into the water, and bury the box. The spring runs grey for an hour, and then clear, and then clearer than any water you have ever seen.

choices.text: Steal it and pour it into a river

ok.log: You take it at night and pour it off a bridge into the river. The water goes grey and then clear. Nobody ever finds out who. In the morning, on the bridge rail where you stood, there is a single chinaberry leaf.

fail.log: You are caught, and beaten, and the box is taken back. But in the struggle the lid came open, and half of it is gone on the wind, and you are glad. (-12 health)

choices.text: Refuse to touch it, and walk out

effects.log: You walk out. The owner calls after you that you are a fool. You are sick in the street. You are not a fool. You are the only person who has ever been in that room and known what the powder was for, and that it was never for seeing.

events.text: Years later a stranger comes to your door: the grandchild of the one who owned the powder. Their grandparent died raving about plots, and their parent too, and they have heard you once knew what the powder was. They want to know whether their family is cursed.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: the powder was the curse

effects.log: "Not your family," you say. "The powder. A horn that was taken, not given, shows you everything and none of it kindly. Nobody can live in that." They weep with relief. You do not tell them how you know. You do not need to: they look at your forehead, once, and seem to understand.

choices.text: Take them north to the spring

effects.log: You take them north, a month's walk, to a clear spring among the birches. You do not explain. They drink, and something in them that has been clenched for their whole life lets go. On the way home they laugh for the first time since you met them.

events.text: Travelling in the far north, at a spring in the birches with ice on its stones, you meet a very small beast: a kid, scaly and curly-maned, with a bud of horn under the curls like the wick of a candle not yet lit. It looks at you with eyes far too old for it, and you know, the way you know a face from a dream, that it remembers everything, and that so, a little, do you.

choices.text: Kneel and let it look at you

effects.log: You kneel in the snow. The kid walks up to you, puts its small cold nose to your forehead, and stands there for a long moment. Then it lays its ears back, very solemnly, and goes back to the spring to drink. You walk on with the strangest feeling that you have been forgiven for something you cannot remember doing.

choices.text: Tell it everything you have done this life

effects.log: You sit by the spring and tell it, the good and the bad, plainly. It listens with its ears up, then down, then up. At the end it butts you once, very gently, on the knee, with its little bud of a horn, and goes. You do not know whether that was a verdict. You think it was a greeting.

events.text: Years after the north, a trapper comes south with a story: the young horned beast of the birch springs has grown, and walks the frontier settling quarrels, and once, asked by a smuggler who it was looking for, turned and looked south, toward the human lands, toward, the trapper says, you.

choices.text: Go north again

effects.log: A month's walk. At the spring it is waiting, half grown now, its horn a hand long. It walks beside you along the frozen stream for a whole day, saying nothing, the way two old friends walk. At dusk it turns back to its spring. You turn south. Neither of you looks back, and neither needs to.

choices.text: Stay, and send it a message by the trapper

effects.log: You give the trapper a message: one true sentence about your life. The trapper comes back the next year and says the beast listened to it with its ears up, and then laid them back, and then went and lay down by the spring, content. You find that you are content too.
